$description: Plenix's own guidance for each page of the Apple Human Interface Guidelines: rules in Plenix's words (never Apple's text), each linked to the HIG section it follows; a property table across iOS, Android and Web; the Web and Android pages each maps to. build-native-guidance.js makes it the design system's data.

ios-components|Text fields.summary: A single-line field for a short value such as a name, an email address or a search term; longer text goes in a text view.

rules.rule: Give every field a visible label; a placeholder is only a hint and disappears as soon as someone types.
Use a secure field for passwords and any other secret.
Size the field to the length of the value you expect, so its width hints at how much to enter.
Stack related fields vertically with even spacing and shared widths, so each label clearly belongs to its field.
Move focus between fields in reading order.
Check a value at the right moment: a format such as an email when the person leaves the field, the rules for a new user name or password while they type.
Read and show numbers through a locale-aware formatter rather than assuming one format.
Show the keyboard that fits the content: email, number, URL or phone.
Offer a Clear button at the trailing end so a value can be erased in one tap.
Use the leading end for an image that states the field's purpose and the trailing end for an extra action.

properties.ios: TextField title / UITextField with a separate UILabel

ios-getting-started|Design principles.summary: The values behind every other Plenix guideline: tools for weighing trade-offs, not a checklist.

rules.rule: Know what the product is for and spend most of the effort on the few features people rely on; cut what does not serve that purpose.
Take people straight to their task, let them leave any guided flow, and make actions reversible so exploring costs nothing.
Explain why you ask for permission or data, collect only what the product needs, and protect it against misuse.
Reuse patterns people already know, keep an element's look and behavior the same everywhere, and confirm every change with clear feedback.
Plan for accessibility from the start, support touch, keyboard, pointer and voice, and keep content and controls where people expect them on every platform.
Show only what the task needs, label with the fewest precise words, and give the screen a clear structure so people know where they are and what comes next.
Prototype early, test in real conditions, discard what fails, and keep the product current after release.
Choose the feeling the product should leave and express it in key moments, without letting decoration slow the task down.

ios-getting-started|Designing for iOS.summary: What sets the iPhone apart: a handheld, medium-size touch screen used in short and long sessions alongside many other apps.

rules.rule: Keep few controls on screen so the main content leads, and reveal secondary actions with one extra step.
Adapt to orientation, Dark Mode and Dynamic Type without breaking, so people can keep the settings they prefer.
Place frequent controls in the middle and bottom of the screen where a thumb reaches, and support swipes for going back and for row actions.
With permission, use device capabilities such as location, payments and biometric sign-in instead of asking people to type data in.

ios-getting-started|Designing for iPadOS.summary: What sets the iPad apart: a large display used at varied distances with touch, keyboard, pointer and Apple Pencil, often beside other apps.

rules.rule: Use the large display for content: avoid modal screens and full-screen hops, and keep controls reachable but out of the content's way.
Set text size and information density from the likely viewing distance and input in use.
Support touch, a hardware keyboard, a trackpad and Apple Pencil, including tasks that combine them.
Keep the layout working through rotation, multitasking sizes, Dark Mode and Dynamic Type, and when the app runs on a Mac.

ios-getting-started|Designing for macOS.summary: What sets the Mac apart: large and multiple displays, precise pointer and keyboard input, long focused sessions in resizable windows.

rules.rule: Use the space to show more content with fewer nested levels and fewer modal steps, while keeping density comfortable to read.
Let people resize, move, hide and show windows, and offer full-screen mode for focused work.
Put every command in the menu bar so people can always find it.
Support precise pointer selection and editing, and keyboard shortcuts for frequent actions and keyboard-only work.
Let people personalize toolbars, window layouts, colors and fonts.

ios-getting-started|Designing for tvOS.summary: What sets Apple TV apart: a very large screen viewed from across the room, driven by a remote, a controller or voice.

rules.rule: Build interactions on the Siri Remote's familiar gestures.
Use the system focus model so the focused item is always obvious and people always know where they are.
Use full-bleed artwork, restrained motion and good audio, and keep everything legible from a distance.
Make sign-in rare and simple, support shared sign-in, and switch profiles when the viewer changes.

ios-getting-started|Designing for vision.summary: What sets Apple Vision Pro apart: an unbounded space for windows, volumes and immersive scenes, controlled with eyes and hands.

rules.rule: Use space, Spatial Audio, immersion, passthrough and eye-and-hand input in ways that feel native to the device.
Give each moment the least immersion it needs; most tasks do not need a fully immersive scene.
Use standard windows with familiar controls for ordinary, UI-centered tasks.
Keep people comfortable: content in their field of view, no jarring or fast motion, input that works with hands at rest, and no need to move around much.
Support shared activities so people can feel present together.

ios-getting-started|Designing for watchO.summary: What sets Apple Watch apart: a small wrist display glanced at many times a day, with the Digital Crown and brief interactions.

rules.rule: Design for glances: one screen with the key information and an action that takes a tap or two.
Keep navigation shallow and use the Digital Crown for vertical scrolling and moving between screens.
Anticipate needs and show what is relevant now, using on-device data.
Put timely data in complications and notifications so people can act without opening the app.
Use background color to carry meaning and materials to show hierarchy.
Make the app work on its own, adding detail beyond its notifications and complications.

ios-getting-started|Designing for games.summary: How a game feels at home on every Apple device: fast start, legible on every screen, native input and room for every player.

rules.rule: Ship enough content to start playing right after install and load the rest in the background.
Pick sensible defaults from the device, its controllers and the player's accessibility settings so no setup is needed to start.
Teach mechanics through play rather than a required written tutorial.
Ask for permission at the moment the feature needs it, and ask for a rating only after the player has spent real time in the game.
Keep text above each platform's minimum size with good contrast, and buttons at least the platform's minimum target (44×44 pt on iOS).
Use resolution-independent art, respect safe areas, and build menus with relative layouts that hold up at every aspect ratio and orientation.
Support each platform's main input, and offer an alternative to physical game controllers.
Never rely on one sense alone, let players adjust text size, controls, motion and sound, and avoid stereotypes in characters and stories.
Use Game Center, cross-device saves, haptics and Spatial Audio where they make the game better.

ios-getting-started|Designing for iPhone.summary: iPhone Duo has an outer and an inner display joined by a hinge; an app that resizes well adapts to every pose with standard components.

rules.rule: Do not design a layout per pose: let size classes carry a compact layout on the outer display and a regular one on the inner display.
Build the layout to resize with margins, safe areas and size classes; avoid fixed widths and anything tied to one display.
Keep the same features, controls and state on both displays and in every pose; the inner display may add one more level of hierarchy.
Keep important content clear of the cameras and the fold, prefer containers that adapt to the fold, and use an even number of grid columns.
Make small adjustments when the device folds rather than rearranging controls.
Use an arrangement view for two views shown side by side or layered, and keep navigation containers outside it.
Keep the system's side placement for toolbars and tab bars, and use safe areas so side controls never cover content.
Put navigation at the top of the side bar, set visibility priorities so frequent and badged items stay visible longest, and group items instead of spacing them by hand.
Give each toolbar item both a title and a symbol, and move custom overflow actions into the system overflow menu.

ios-foundations|Accessibility.summary: Make every task usable by people of any ability and with any way of using the device: intuitive, perceivable and adaptable.

rules.rule: Let text and icons grow to at least 200 percent (140 percent on watchOS), ideally through Dynamic Type.
Meet WCAG AA contrast in light and dark, and offer a higher-contrast scheme when Increase Contrast is on.
Never use color as the only signal; add a shape, icon or text.
Describe every element and its content for VoiceOver.
Provide captions, subtitles, audio descriptions or transcripts for media, and pair audio cues with haptics and visual cues.
Make controls at least the platform minimum size (44×44 pt on iOS) with room between them so people do not hit the wrong one.
Use simple gestures for frequent actions and offer an on-screen control for every gesture.
Label elements so Voice Control, Switch Control and other assistive technologies work, and test with them.
Make every feature reachable with the keyboard alone, and do not override system keyboard shortcuts.
Avoid views that dismiss on a timer, never autoplay media without controls, and respect Dim Flashing Lights.
When Reduce Motion is on, replace zooming, sliding and bouncing animations with fades or no motion.
On visionOS, keep content in the field of view, slow peripheral motion, avoid head-locked content and large repeated gestures.

ios-foundations|App icons.summary: The app's mark on the Home Screen and across the system: one simple, layered image that the system shapes and lights.

rules.rule: Build the icon from a background and foreground layers with crisp edges, and prefer vector art for the layers.
Supply unmasked square (rectangular on tvOS) layers and let the system apply the corner or circle mask.
Keep the main subject centered so masking never cuts it.
Express one idea with few shapes on a simple background, and keep the design the same on every platform.
Avoid text, photos, screenshots and copies of UI controls; use text only when it is essential to the brand.
Leave highlights, shadows, bevels and blurs to the system rather than painting them in.
Keep the same core features in the default, dark, clear and tinted versions, deriving the dark one from the light one.
On tvOS, keep a safe zone around the content so focus scaling does not crop it.
On watchOS, avoid a black background so the icon does not vanish into the display.

ios-foundations|Branding.summary: How to express the brand inside the app without getting in the way of content or familiar behavior.

rules.rule: Carry the brand's voice and tone through all app text.
Use the accent color sparingly, for primary actions and status, not on every control.
A brand font must stay legible at every size and support bold text and Dynamic Type; keep body text in a highly legible face.
Brand through familiar components and standard placement, symbols and navigation rather than custom behavior.
Let branding defer to content: show the logo only where it gives context, and never use the launch screen as a brand moment.
Keep Apple trademarks out of the app name and images.

ios-foundations|Color.summary: How to use system and custom color so meaning stays consistent and legible in every appearance and setting.

rules.rule: Give each color one meaning across the app; never reuse the interactive color for static text.
Define every custom color for light, dark and increased contrast, even if the app ships in one appearance.
Check colors on several devices and in bright and dim light, and adjust nearby colors for artwork and translucent bars.
Use the system color picker when people choose colors.
Never use color alone to identify, mark interactivity or convey essential information; pair it with text or a shape.
Check that colors carry the intended meaning in other cultures.
Use system colors through their API, never their documented values, and use each semantic color only for its stated role.
Tint Liquid Glass only for emphasis such as a primary action, color the background rather than the label, and never tint many controls.
Over colorful content, keep bar controls monochrome and keep the resting state of the content legible behind controls.
Embed color profiles in images, use Display P3 where wide color helps, and supply sRGB variants when P3 colors would clip or merge.
On iOS, use the primary, secondary and tertiary background colors for levels of grouping, and the grouped set for grouped lists.
On tvOS, never show focus with color alone; use scale and motion.
On visionOS, use color sparingly on glass, prefer it in bold text and large areas, and keep brightness balanced in immersive scenes.
On watchOS, use background color to inform rather than decorate, and avoid it on screens that stay up a long time.

ios-foundations|Dark Mode.summary: The dark system appearance: apps follow the person's choice and stay legible and well-separated in both appearances.

rules.rule: Follow the system appearance by default and switch live when it changes; an in-app override, where offered, defaults to System.
Check legibility in both appearances, including with Increase Contrast and Reduce Transparency on.
Use a permanently dark interface only for rare cases such as immersive media viewing.
Use semantic colors that adapt, give every custom color a light and a dark value, and never hard-code colors.
Keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more in both appearances, aiming for 7:1 for small custom text.
Dim content images with white backgrounds slightly so they do not glare in dark surroundings.
Prefer symbols tinted with dynamic colors, and supply separate light and dark assets when one image does not work in both.
Use the system label colors and system text views rather than drawing text yourself.
On iOS, use the system backgrounds so popovers and sheets get the lighter elevated color automatically.
On macOS, add slight transparency to neutral custom backgrounds so desktop tinting shows through; never to colored states.

properties.android: darkTheme parameter of the app theme

ios-foundations|Icons.summary: Interface icons (glyphs): simple single-color shapes that name an item, action or mode, unlike the richer app icon.

rules.rule: Draw a simple, widely recognized metaphor tied directly to the action or content it stands for.
Keep size, detail, stroke weight and perspective the same across every icon in the product, and match icon weight to adjacent text.
Center asymmetric icons optically, building the correction into the asset's padding rather than nudging it in layout.
Skip a separate selected version when a standard component already shows the selected state.
Use gender-neutral figures and culture-neutral images; include letters only when essential, localize them, and provide a mirrored version for right-to-left text.
Ship custom icons as vectors (SVG or PDF), never as fixed-size bitmaps.
Give every icon that carries meaning an accessibility label; hide purely decorative ones from assistive technology.
Use the icon set's standard symbol for common actions such as edit, select, search, share, account and ordering, so they mean the same thing everywhere.
On macOS, give custom document types a simple document icon that stays recognizable down to 16 px.

properties.web: plx-icon with a Material Symbols name

ios-foundations|Images.summary: How to supply bitmap and vector images so they stay sharp and true in color on every display.

rules.rule: Provide every bitmap at each scale factor the supported devices use (@2x and @3x on iPhone).
Design at 1x and scale up, keeping vector control points on whole values so they stay on the pixel grid.
Choose the format by content: vectors for flat interface art, PNG for lossless graphics, JPEG or HEIC for photos.
Embed a color profile in every image and check images on real devices for blur, stretching and compression.
On tvOS, use layered images with an opaque background and text in the front layer for focusable artwork, with a safe zone so focus motion never crops key content.
On visionOS, prefer vector art, and show spatial photos in their own view rather than inline with other content.
On watchOS, avoid transparency except in template images, and use one autoscaling PDF for all screen sizes.

ios-foundations|Immersive experiences.summary: visionOS levels of immersion, from windows in the Shared Space to a Full Space that partly or fully replaces the surroundings.

rules.rule: Pick the immersion style that fits the content: dimmed passthrough, mixed, progressive or full.
Launch in the Shared Space or in mixed immersion, and let people raise immersion themselves.
Reserve deeper immersion for the moments that gain from it, and draw attention with subtle cues first.
Support the accessibility features people use, offering more than one way to use the experience.
Keep content in the field of view, never require people to walk around, and do not let mixed content block the view of the room.
Change immersion gently and only on the person's request, with a clear exit control that says where it leads.
Make virtual hands follow the real ones at a natural size, and fade them out if tracking drops.
Build an expansive, grounded environment with subtle motion, few distractions and a soundscape that yields to other audio.

ios-foundations|Inclusion.summary: Design words, images and experiences that welcome people of every background, identity and ability.

rules.rule: Review the product from many perspectives, aiming to welcome people rather than merely avoid offense.
Address people as you, keep we for the company, write plainly, define technical terms, and avoid idioms and humor that do not translate.
Make the product usable without prior knowledge, with optional onboarding people can skip.
Avoid needless gendered words and figures; ask for gender only when required, with inclusive options and a way to decline.
Show a real range of people, places and circumstances, never stereotyped roles.
Check design decisions, such as family models or security questions, for assumptions that leave people out.
Support the system accessibility features and write about disability people-first, without using it to describe something negative.
Internationalize text, dates, numbers and currency from the start, and check what colors mean in each locale.

ios-foundations|Layout.summary: How to arrange content and controls so hierarchy is clear and the layout adapts to every size, orientation and setting.

rules.rule: Put the most important items at the top and leading side, following reading order, with components that mirror for right-to-left languages.
Align items to make them scannable, indent to show subordination, and group related items with space, containers or separators.
Reveal detail progressively through disclosure, menus or nested views instead of showing every option at once.
Set controls apart from content with the platform's control layer rather than solid backing colors, and let full-screen backgrounds run beneath bars and sidebars.
Keep the layout familiar through rotation, window resizing, extra displays and device changes by respecting safe areas, margins and layout guides.
Reflow for larger text: stack side-by-side views and let rows grow so text is never cut off or overlapping.
Test the smallest and largest layouts, other languages and the largest text sizes first.
Choose the layout from the available space (size class or window class), never from device type or orientation.
Keep the same features at every size; only how much is visible may change, for example a tab bar becoming a sidebar.
Keep content and controls inside the safe area so hardware features and system bars never cover them.
On macOS, keep controls and critical information away from the bottom of a window and the camera housing.
On tvOS, inset content 60 pt top and bottom and 80 pt at the sides, with spacing that lets focused items grow without overlap.
On visionOS, support window resizing, use 3D content sparingly in windows, and open supplemental content in an adjacent window rather than an ornament.
On watchOS, put no more than three icon buttons or two text buttons in a row.

ios-foundations|Materials.summary: Translucent layers that separate controls and navigation from content while letting the content show through.

rules.rule: Use Liquid Glass only for the control and navigation layer above content, never for content itself such as app backgrounds.
Let standard components supply Liquid Glass, and add it to custom controls only for the most important functional elements.
Use the regular variant by default and for text-heavy components; use clear only over rich media, with a dimming layer when the media is bright.
Choose a material by its purpose, not by the color it appears to give, and put vibrant system colors on top of it.
Use thicker materials where fine text needs contrast and thinner ones where keeping the background in view matters.
On iOS, avoid the quaternary label vibrancy on thin and ultra-thin materials, where its contrast is too low.
On macOS, test where vibrancy helps in custom views and pick the blending mode that suits the design.
On visionOS, prefer translucency to opaque fills in windows, and use the system vibrancy levels for text hierarchy.
On watchOS, keep the default material behind full-screen modal views.

ios-foundations|Motion.summary: How to use animation to give feedback and explain change without distracting people or making them uncomfortable.

rules.rule: Animate only with a purpose; never add motion for its own sake.
Never use motion as the only carrier of information, and honor Reduce Motion by fading or removing movement.
Make feedback motion follow the gesture and its physical logic: a view leaves the way it came in.
Keep feedback animations short and precise, and leave frequent interactions without extra motion.
Never make people wait for an animation to finish before they can act.
In games, hold a steady frame rate by default and let people trade visual quality for performance or battery.
On visionOS, avoid motion in peripheral vision, rotating worlds and slow sustained oscillation; fade objects out and in to relocate them and give a stationary frame of reference.

ios-foundations|Privacy.summary: How to ask for, use and protect personal data so people stay informed and in control.

rules.rule: Ask only for the data a feature needs, as narrowly as possible, and say plainly how it is used.
Process data on the device where possible, and rely on the system's privacy and security protections.
Request a permission when the person first uses the feature that needs it, not at launch unless the app cannot work without it.
Write the usage description as one short, specific, active sentence in sentence case that says what the access is for.
If a screen comes before the system prompt, give it a single button such as Continue that opens the prompt, with no Allow wording and no way to skip the prompt.
Show the system tracking prompt before collecting any tracking data, and never steer the choice with incentives or look-alike screens.
Use the location button for one-time location sharing tied to a task, customizing only its allowed attributes and keeping its text untruncated at every size and language.
Prefer passkeys and system sign-in over passwords, add two-factor or biometric checks where passwords remain, and keep secrets in the keychain, never in plain files.
On macOS, sign with Developer ID, use the app sandbox, and never assume who is signed in.
On visionOS, request permission for ARKit data such as hand tracking, and replace camera-dependent features with an import option.

properties.ios: Info.plist usage description keys (for example NSCameraUsageDescription)
properties.android: permission rationale shown before the request
properties.web: explanation shown before the browser permission prompt

ios-foundations|Right to left.summary: How the interface mirrors for right-to-left languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, and what must not mirror.

rules.rule: Align short text with the interface direction, but align paragraphs of three or more lines with their own language.
Give every item in a list the same alignment, even items in another script.
Keep each number's digits as written; only a sequence of numbers that expresses progress or order flips direction.
Mirror controls that show progress or move through an ordered flow, such as sliders, progress bars, back and next.
Keep the direction of a control that points to a real direction or a place on screen.
Do not flip photos or artwork; reverse the order of images only when the order carries meaning.
Mirror icons that show text, reading direction or forward and backward motion; never mirror logos, universal marks such as the checkmark, or real-world objects like clocks.
Localize icons that contain letters, and in complex icons decide per part, such as a badge, whether it should mirror.

ios-foundations|SF Symbols.summary: Apple's symbol library for interface icons on Apple platforms, with rendering modes, weights, variants and animations.

rules.rule: Color symbols with system colors and pick the rendering mode (monochrome, hierarchical, palette or multicolor) that stays legible at its size and background.
Use variable color to show a value that changes, such as strength or level, never to show depth.
Match a symbol's weight to the adjacent text and use its scale to adjust emphasis.
Use outline beside text, fill for selection and emphasis, slash for unavailable, and enclosed shapes for legibility at small sizes; let the container choose where it can.
Animate a symbol only when the motion says something specific, such as an action happening or a status changing, and keep animations few.
Only when the set has nothing suitable, build a custom symbol from a similar symbol's template, matching its detail, weight and alignment, and test it with every animation.
Give every custom symbol an accessibility label, and never alter or copy symbols that depict Apple products.

ios-foundations|Spatial layout.summary: How to place content in three dimensions on visionOS using field of view, depth and scale.

rules.rule: Center important content in the field of view and anchor it in the room, never to the wearer's head.
Use depth to show hierarchy on large elements, with accurate cues, and keep text and small controls flat.
Limit how many depth levels people must refocus between.
Keep interactive content at dynamic scale; reserve fixed scale for non-interactive objects that must look life-size.
Open few windows, favor indirect gestures, and keep direct touch for nearby objects used briefly.
Space interactive elements so their centers are at least 60 pt apart and nothing interactive overlaps.
Make the experience usable without moving, and place floor-standing immersive content on a plane aligned to the floor.

ios-foundations|Typography.summary: How to choose and size type so text is legible, shows hierarchy and scales with the person's text-size setting.

rules.rule: Keep text at or above each platform's default and minimum sizes (iOS body 17 pt, minimum 11 pt), going larger for thin weights.
Avoid ultralight, thin and light weights for interface text, and test legibility on every target device.
Show hierarchy with weight, size and color, and keep it intact at every text size.
Use as few typefaces as possible.
When text grows, enlarge the content people read first; secondary chrome such as tab titles need not grow as much.
Build on the platform's text styles and adjust them with traits such as bold or leading; never use tight leading for three or more lines.
A custom font, such as the Plenix DM Sans, must stay legible at the minimum sizes and support Dynamic Type and Bold Text like the system font.
Make the layout work at every text size, including the accessibility sizes, with meaningful icons growing alongside the text.
Avoid truncation at large sizes: let labels wrap, stack text above secondary items, reduce columns, and keep primary elements at the top.
On macOS, which has no Dynamic Type, use the system font variants that match standard controls where text sits beside them.
On visionOS, prefer flat text with strong contrast, bold for text without a background, and turn labels in space to face the viewer.

ios-foundations|Writing.summary: How to write interface text that is clear, consistent, inclusive and suited to the moment.

rules.rule: Define the product's voice and a shared word list, then vary tone with the situation: plain for problems, warmer for success.
Use as few plain words as possible, free of jargon and gendered terms, written with accessibility and translation in mind.
Lead each screen with its most important information and split separate ideas across steps.
Label buttons with verbs and links with descriptive words, never "click here".
Apply one capitalization style per element type everywhere; Plenix uses sentence case.
Use the same step labels throughout a multi-step flow and end it with a clear completion label such as Done.
Avoid we and unneeded possessives such as my and your, and name gestures correctly for the device (tap, not click, on touch).
Give empty states a next step with a button or link, and keep crucial information out of them.
Place an error message next to the problem, without blame or interjections, and say how to fix it.
Describe what a setting does when on, link straight to settings instead of describing the path, and label every field with a hint for its format.

ios-patterns|Charting data.summary: Use a chart when people need to see a trend, a state or a comparison in a dataset; plain values that people only look up belong in a list or table.

rules.rule: Chart data only when there is a finding to show; give each chart one clear takeaway.
Start with a simple chart and let people reveal more detail or subsets on request instead of packing everything in at once.
Make every chart accessible: label its values and parts for assistive technology and let people move through the data points.
Prefer familiar chart types such as bar and line; when a chart is unusual, teach people how to read it the first time they see it.
Add a title, a one-line summary and annotations that point at what matters; this text supports, and never replaces, the accessibility labels.
Size a chart for its job: small for a glanceable preview, large enough for readable labels and interaction when people explore it.
Keep charts with a similar purpose in one type and style, and change style only to signal a real difference.
When several views show the same dataset, keep the chart type, colors, marks and annotations the same so people see it is one dataset.

ios-patterns|Collaboration and sharing.summary: Let people send content or start working on it together through the system share sheet and the Collaboration button, with a short set of permission choices.

rules.rule: Put the Share button where people expect it, usually in the toolbar, and open the system share sheet from it.
Configure the share sheet for the sharing modes the app really supports, such as sending a copy or inviting collaborators.
Summarize the access rules in a short phrase, and keep the permission choices few and grouped so they read at a glance.
Once content is shared, place the Collaboration button beside Share so people can always see who has access.
Add custom items to the collaboration popover only when they are essential while working together.
Post notable collaboration events, such as edits, mentions or membership changes, with a link that opens the right place in the app.
On visionOS, expect window sharing to pause while the app runs in a Full Space, and plan the shared experience around it.
On watchOS, use the system share link to present sharing rather than a custom sheet.

ios-patterns|Drag and drop.summary: Let people move or copy content by dragging it from a source to a destination, with clear feedback the whole way and another route for anyone who cannot drag.

rules.rule: Support drag and drop wherever people are likely to try it; system text controls provide it for free.
Offer another way to do every drag action, such as a menu command or an accessibility action.
Move content within one container and copy it between containers, unless another outcome is clearly safer for the data.
Allow several selected items to be dragged together.
Make a drop undoable; when it cannot be undone, confirm before completing it.
Provide the dragged data in several formats from richest to simplest so each destination can take the best it supports.
Show a translucent preview of the dragged content from the moment the drag starts until the drop.
Highlight a destination only while content is over it and only if it accepts the content; show a not-allowed cue otherwise.
When a drop fails or lands on an invalid target, animate the item back to its source or away so the failure is visible.
Auto-scroll a long destination while the item is held over it, and stop once the pointer leaves.
Take the richest format you can use and keep only the relevant part of what was dropped.
Show progress or a placeholder when dropped content takes time to arrive or starts a task.
Keep dropped content selected in the destination and clear the selection in the source.
On iPadOS, let people add items to a drag that is already in progress and accept several drops at once.
On macOS, let people drag from an inactive window without activating it, show a count badge for multi-item drags and change the pointer to show the drop result.
On visionOS, open a window that handles content dropped into empty space when the app can display it.

properties.web: draggable attribute and the Plenix drag-and-drop engine
Drop target pattern (dragover and drop events)

properties.ios: accessibilityDragPoint / accessibilityDropPoint, or a menu command
properties.web: keyboard move commands (Accessible drag and drop)

ios-patterns|Entering data.summary: Ask people for as little input as possible and make what remains quick to enter, with any input method they prefer.

rules.rule: Get what the system already knows, or can share with permission, instead of asking people to type it.
Make each requested value clear with a label and, where useful, a hint or a sensible default.
Mask sensitive values with a secure field, and never fill in a password for people; use the keychain or biometrics instead.
Offer a picker, menu or other choice control instead of free text whenever the answers are known.
Accept pasted and dropped values in input fields.
Check values as soon as they are entered and report problems right away; use a formatter for numbers, currency and percentages.
Make clear which values are required, and keep the Next or Continue action unavailable until they are provided.
On macOS, show the full value of a truncated field in an expansion tooltip on hover.

ios-patterns|Feedback.summary: Tell people what is happening, what worked, what failed and what is risky, with an interruption level that matches the importance of the message.

rules.rule: Deliver feedback in more than one way, such as text plus color, sound or haptics, so it reaches people who are not looking or use VoiceOver.
Show status quietly next to the thing it describes so people can check it without leaving their task.
Reserve alerts for critical, preferably actionable, information; frequent alerts lose their force.
Warn before an action that would lose data unexpectedly and irreversibly, but not when losing it is the point of the action.
Confirm completion only for significant tasks; for routine ones, speak up only on failure.
When a command cannot run, say so and explain why.
On watchOS, avoid indeterminate loading indicators; promise a notification when the work finishes instead.

ios-patterns|File management.summary: Help people create, open, save and preview their documents in ways that match the system file browser they already know.

rules.rule: Offer New and Open as menu commands with their keyboard shortcuts, and always include an Add (+) button for a new document.
If you build a custom file browser, open it at the most relevant location but let people reach the rest of the file system.
Save automatically while people edit and when they close or leave a document, so work is never lost unless they cancel or delete it.
Hide file extensions by default, let people show them, and honor that choice in every open and save view.
Preview files the app cannot open with a Quick Look viewer instead of sending people elsewhere.
Provide a Quick Look generator for custom file types so other apps and search can preview them.
On iOS and iPadOS, if you use the document launcher, give its two buttons the main actions, keep the background plain and the motion gentle, and keep the title and buttons clear of accessories.
In a file provider extension, list only files that fit the current task, let people pick a destination when exporting or moving, and add no second toolbar.
On macOS, use the standard open and save panels unless there is a strong reason not to; a custom one still offers recent files, filtering, and name, format and location choices.
On macOS, when autosave is off, mark unsaved documents and ask to save on close or quit; show no unsaved mark when autosave is on.

ios-patterns|Going full screen.summary: Offer a full-screen mode for immersive or focused work such as games, media and deep tasks, and leave people in control of it.

rules.rule: Offer full screen when people benefit from focus or immersion: games, photos and video, long focused tasks.
Adapt the layout subtly to the larger space, keeping the same items, and never resize the window from code.
Keep the essential controls available, or easy to reveal, so people can finish their task without leaving full screen.
Outside games, keep the Dock reachable in full screen on iPadOS and macOS.
Pause playback or play when the person leaves, and pick up from the same point on their return.
Let people decide when to leave full screen; never exit it automatically.
Hide bars while content is the focus, bring them back with a familiar tap, swipe or pointer move, and keep controls needed for navigation visible.
On iOS and iPadOS, keep the standard single swipe to leave; require two only when accidental exits are a real problem.
On macOS, use the system full-screen mode, let people enter it with the standard button, menu item or shortcut, and never change the display mode for them.

ios-patterns|Launching.summary: Get people from opening the app to a usable first screen as fast as possible, and put them back where they left off.

rules.rule: Launch fast; people expect to start in a second or two.
Provide a launch screen on the platforms that require one: iOS, iPadOS and tvOS.
Put any branded splash graphic at the start of onboarding, or right after launch, never in the launch screen.
Restore the previous state on relaunch, down to scroll position and window layout.
Make the launch screen nearly identical to the first screen, in the current orientation and appearance, so nothing flashes when it is replaced.
Keep text, logos and advertising off the launch screen; it cannot be localized and is not a branding moment.
On iOS and iPadOS, launch in the device's current orientation, or in the only one supported, and handle both landscape directions.
On tvOS, consider starting live or recent content automatically after a short idle moment in a live-viewing app.
On visionOS, open first in the Shared Space and let people choose when to enter a Full Space.

ios-patterns|Live-viewing apps.summary: For apps that stream live TV: put live content first, make it obviously live, and keep guide browsing and recording close to playback.

rules.rule: Put live content up front so playback is at most one tap from launch.
Mark live content clearly, with a badge or symbol, so it never looks like on-demand content.
Show how far a live program has progressed before people join it.
Keep playback the primary action and list secondary actions, such as start over and record, in the same order everywhere.
If you let people browse channels during playback, use a subtle, legible footer that marks the current channel and opens and closes with matching gestures.
Respond instantly to a channel change, and stop live audio when people leave the live context.
Open the program guide on what is playing now, make it fast to page through, group it in familiar categories, and keep playback running while people browse.
Let people record from the info panel and from a program's detail view, choose exactly what to record, and manage storage automatically.

ios-patterns|Loading.summary: Keep loading from blocking people: show content or placeholders early, load in the background and say how long it will take.

rules.rule: Show something right away, such as placeholders, and replace it as real content arrives; a blank screen reads as a fault.
Load in the background so people can keep doing other things while they wait.
When a wait is unavoidably long, fill it with something useful such as tips, timed to the expected duration.
Download large assets in the background at quiet times rather than during install or launch.
When loading takes more than a moment, show a progress indicator: determinate when the duration is known, indeterminate when it is not.
In a game, a custom loading view that matches the game's style can replace the standard indicator.
On watchOS, aim to show content immediately; if it needs a second or two, a loading indicator still beats a blank screen.

ios-patterns|Managing accounts.summary: Require an account only when the core features need one, make signing in clear and password-light, and make deleting the account as easy as creating it.

rules.rule: In the sign-in view, explain briefly why an account is needed and what people gain from it.
Let people explore the app first and ask them to sign in only when a task actually needs an account.
Prefer Sign in with Apple or passkeys; if passwords remain, require two-factor authentication.
Name the sign-in method on its button, and mention only methods the current device supports.
Do not add an in-app switch for biometric sign-in, and do not call the account secret a passcode.
If people can create an account in the app, let them delete it, not only deactivate it, from a place that is easy to find.
Keep in-app and web deletion equally simple, say when deletion will be complete and notify people when it is.
Offer scheduled deletion alongside immediate deletion, and explain what happens to subscriptions and billing.
For a TV provider app, use system-level provider sign-in, hide sign-out when people are signed in that way, and never send people to privacy settings to sign out.
On tvOS, ask for as little typing as possible: sign in from another device, and use the shared-account profile without asking each time.
On watchOS, sync the keychain through iCloud so credentials and settings fill in automatically.

ios-patterns|Managing notifications.summary: Send notifications only with permission, at an honest urgency level, and give people control over them inside the app.

rules.rule: Classify each notification as communication or non-communication, and give every non-communication notification a system interruption level.
Use the Critical level only for urgent health and safety information, and only with the entitlement it requires.
Set the urgency of each notification honestly; never raise the level to interrupt with low-priority news.
Use Time Sensitive only for events happening now or within the hour.
Send promotional notifications only after an explicit opt-in that says what will be sent, and never at the Time Sensitive level.
Provide an in-app settings screen where people can change their notification choices.
On watchOS, expect the iPhone notification settings to apply, with quick per-notification options on the watch.

ios-patterns|Modality.summary: Present content modally only to focus people on a short, distinct task or a critical decision, and always make the way out obvious.

rules.rule: Use a modal view only when focus or a decision clearly benefits people; it interrupts their context and must be dismissed.
Keep modal tasks short and simple so people do not lose track of the task they left.
Avoid deep navigation inside a modal view; if it needs subviews, give one path and no buttons that look like the dismiss button.
Use a full-screen modal style for media, camera views and complex multistep editing.
Always provide an obvious way to dismiss, following the platform convention for its placement.
If dismissing would discard content people created, confirm first and offer a way to save it.
Title the modal view with the task it performs.
Close one modal view before opening another, and never show two alerts at once.

ios-patterns|Multitasking.summary: Expect people to switch apps and windows at any moment: save and restore context, pause what needs attention and finish what they started.

rules.rule: Be ready to save and restore context at any time, since people can switch away whenever they like.
Pause games and media when people switch away and let them continue exactly where they were.
Handle audio interruptions: pause for a long interruption and duck or pause, then recover, for a short one.
Finish tasks people started, such as downloads or exports, in the background.
Notify on completion only for important tasks; let routine ones wait until people return.
On iPhone, support Picture in Picture for video and calls so they continue over other apps.
On iPadOS, adapt to any window size, since people can resize and tile windows and the app is not told which arrangement they chose.
On macOS, assume several apps and windows are open at once and keep window states clearly distinguishable.
On tvOS, support Picture in Picture where it applies so people can browse while watching.
On visionOS, leave window edges alone, keep video playing when people look away, and expect audio to duck when the app is not Now Playing.

ios-patterns|Offering help.summary: Give help that fits the task at hand, in the platform's terms, from short inline tips to tutorials, and keep it easy to dismiss.

rules.rule: Match the help to the task: an inline note for a simple step, a tutorial for a complex goal; tie it to what people are doing now and make it easy to skip.
Use the words and images of the current platform and input device, such as tap on touch and click on a Mac.
Write inclusive help content.
Do not explain standard controls; explain what they do in this app, and teach unusual interactions with a quick visual.
Choose a popover tip to keep content flowing or an inline tip to keep the surroundings visible, and use tips only for features of three steps or fewer.
Keep a tip to one or two action-oriented sentences with no promotion.
Show a tip only to people who would benefit, and limit how often tips appear.
Add a recognizable filled symbol when it helps, without repeating an image the tip points at, and add a button that leads to settings or more detail when useful.
On macOS and visionOS, write tooltips that describe only the indicated control, start with a verb, skip the control's name and stay under about 75 characters in sentence case.

ios-patterns|Onboarding.summary: If people need an introduction after launch, keep it short, hands-on and skippable, and put off any setup that can wait.

rules.rule: Teach by letting people try the real action safely rather than by showing instructions.
Prefer small tips shown in context, next to the part of the interface they describe, over one up-front flow.
If an up-front flow is unavoidable, keep it brief and enjoyable, with little to remember.
Make a tutorial optional; once skipped, do not show it again on launch but keep it reachable from help or settings.
Teach the app, not the device or the operating system.
Show a splash graphic only briefly, ship enough content that people never wait for downloads, and leave license text to the store.
Use sensible defaults and postpone optional setup and customization.
Ask for a permission during onboarding only when the app cannot work without it, and explain why; otherwise ask when the feature is first used.
Wait until people have used the app before asking for a rating or a purchase.

ios-patterns|Playing audio.summary: Make app sound follow the person's volume, silent mode, output device and other apps' audio exactly as they expect.

rules.rule: Balance your own sound levels, but never change the system volume; it always sets the final output.
Let people send audio to another output, using the system volume view for level and route.
Pick the audio session category that matches how the app uses sound, so mixing, background play and silent mode behave as expected.
Respond to external playback controls only while the app is playing or clearly in an audio context, and never give them a new meaning.
Build custom player controls only for commands the system does not offer.
When temporary audio ends, signal it so other apps can resume.
Decide how the app reacts to an interruption, and never re-enable a microphone the system muted without people knowing.
After an interruption, resume media playback only when the interruption was resumable; a game can simply resume.
On iOS and iPadOS, play short sounds and vibrations through the system sound services.
On macOS, expect notification sounds to mix with other audio.
On tvOS, play sound only in response to something people do.
On visionOS, use sound generously, give custom elements their own feedback sounds, use Spatial Audio with varied, object-anchored sources, and never carry meaning by sound alone.
On watchOS, encode audio as 64 kbps HE-AAC and offer the Now Playing view for control.

ios-patterns|Playing haptics.summary: Use touch feedback sparingly and consistently, to reinforce what people see and hear, never as the only signal.

rules.rule: Use each system haptic only for its documented meaning; for anything else, use a generic or custom pattern.
Tie each haptic to one kind of cause and use it the same way everywhere.
Pair haptics with matching visual and sound feedback, with intensity and sharpness that fit the animation.
Use haptics rarely, and prefer short ones for discrete events over long continuous patterns outside games.
Let people turn haptics off, and keep the app fully usable without them.
Avoid haptics while the camera, microphone or motion sensors are in use.
Build custom patterns from transient and continuous events, varying intensity and sharpness to match the context.
On iPhone, rely on the haptics standard controls play, and use the notification, impact or selection feedback generators for the matching events.
On macOS, play trackpad haptics only in response to a drag or a force click.
On watchOS, use the built-in haptic types for their stated meanings and let the Digital Crown detents work as the system provides them.

ios-patterns|Playing video.summary: Play video with the system player whenever possible, at its true aspect ratio, and get people into and out of playback without detours.

rules.rule: Use the system video player; if a custom one is unavoidable, make it behave like the system player.
Deliver video at its original aspect ratio, with no letterbox or pillarbox bars baked into the frame.
Add title, description and artwork when they help, without covering the picture.
Support the playback interactions people expect on each input device, such as Space to play or pause.
On tvOS, keep any added transport control or content tab to the most useful actions and short information.
Handle secondary audio so sound from two sources never mixes when people switch playback modes.
When opened from the TV app, go from a black screen straight into the chosen content, resume without asking, and use the requested profile.
Skip the loading screen when content loads fast; otherwise show a plain black screen with a centered spinner only until playback can start.
When playback ends or is exited, show the detail view of what was playing with a resume option, prepared in advance.
On tvOS, keep logos and passive overlays small and translucent, and pause before showing an interactive overlay that people can dismiss.
On visionOS, let people start playback, begin in a small resizable window with the surroundings visible, never auto-start immersive video, and keep the controls unobstructed.
On visionOS, supply a thumbnail track for scrubbing, keep inline video two-dimensional, and use the RealityKit player for transitional video without controls.
On watchOS, keep clips to about 30 seconds at the recommended size and encoding, with a poster image that shows the content and does not look like a control.

ios-patterns|Printing.summary: Make printing easy to find, offer it only when something can be printed, and use the system print options.

rules.rule: Put Print where the platform expects it: the File menu on macOS, a share or action button on iOS and iPadOS.
Disable or remove the print action when there is nothing to print or no printer is available.
Offer page range, copies and two-sided printing through the system print view when the printer supports them.
On macOS, put app-specific options in a named custom category of the print panel, and use a page setup dialog only for per-document page settings the system does not already cover.
On macOS, make dependencies between options visible, tuck advanced options behind a disclosure, preview the effect of settings and remember them with the document.

ios-patterns|Ratings and reviews.summary: Ask for a rating only after people have seen the app's value, at a natural pause, rarely, and with the system prompt.

rules.rule: Ask for a rating only after people show engagement, such as finishing a significant task; never on first launch or in onboarding.
Never interrupt a task or a game to ask; wait for a natural break.
Space rating requests out by several days at minimum, and repeat one only after the person has used the app more.
Use the system rating prompt, which already limits how often it appears.
Reset the summary rating with a new version only when current ratings matter more than a higher count.

ios-patterns|Searching.summary: Give people one obvious place to search, show what is being searched, help them type less, and expose app content to system search.

rules.rule: When search matters, give it a prominent home, such as a toolbar field or its own tab.
Offer one search that finds everything, adding a local filter-style search only for clearly separate sections.
Always show the current search scope through the placeholder, a scope control or the title.
Show recent searches before typing and suggestions while typing.
Consider privacy before showing search history, and let people clear it.
Index app content with descriptive metadata so Spotlight can find it, and describe the metadata of custom file types.
Use Spotlight for advanced file search inside the app, prefer the system open and save views, and provide Quick Look previews for custom files.

ios-patterns|Settings.summary: Choose good defaults so few settings are needed; keep general options in a settings area and task options where the task happens.

rules.rule: Pick defaults that suit most people so they can start without adjusting anything.
Offer as few settings as possible.
Open settings the expected way, such as Command-Comma in an app or Escape in a game.
Detect what the app can detect, such as a controller or Dark Mode, instead of asking for it in settings.
Honor system-wide settings and never duplicate them, such as accessibility or authentication, in the app's settings.
Keep the settings area for general options people change rarely.
Put options that affect one view, such as show, hide, sort or filter, in that view rather than in settings.
Add only the rarest options to the system Settings app, and link to them from the app.
On macOS, open settings from the app menu, not a toolbar button, in a window with fixed pane buttons, a title naming the pane, disabled minimize and zoom, and the last pane restored.
On watchOS, keep the few essential options in the main view, low on the screen, or behind a More menu.

ios-patterns|Undo and redo.summary: Let people reverse recent actions many times over, and make each undo and redo predictable and visible.

rules.rule: Say what an undo or redo will do, for example in the menu item label or the undo alert.
Show the result of each undo and redo, scrolling to it when it is off screen.
Allow multiple levels of undo, back to at least the last open or save.
Consider undoing a series of related small changes as one step, or reverting everything since the last save.
Add undo and redo buttons only when needed, in a toolbar with the standard symbols.
On iOS and iPadOS, keep the standard undo gestures, and name the action in the undo alert in a word or two.
On macOS, Undo and Redo lead the Edit menu, with Command-Z and Shift-Command-Z.

ios-patterns|Workouts.summary: For fitness apps on Apple Watch, iPhone and iPad: show the metrics that matter during a session, with large controls and a clear summary at the end.

rules.rule: On watchOS, use a workout session and show the metrics people care about, such as time, distance and calories, with relevant controls like laps.
Show nothing unrelated to the workout while it is running.
Make an active workout recognizable at a glance, with live values and a distinct layout.
Make pause, resume and stop easy to find and tap, and confirm clearly when a session starts or stops.
When a sensor cannot measure, explain what is still being recorded, in terms like the system Workout app uses.
End with a summary of the recorded data, and discard or ask about sessions that last only seconds.
Keep text large and high-contrast so it reads while moving, and use Activity rings only for their defined meaning.

ios-components|Charts.summary: A chart turns a set of values into marks on a plot so people can see a trend, a comparison or an outlier at a glance.

rules.rule: Choose the mark for the question: bars to compare categories or totals, lines for change over time, points to show how two values relate and where the outliers are.
Combine mark types only when the mix explains more, such as points on a line to call out single readings.
Fix the axis range when its ends carry meaning (0 to 100 percent); otherwise let the range follow the data so the marks fill the plot.
Start a bar chart at zero, but let other charts start where the differences that matter stay visible.
Use round, familiar tick steps and only as many grid lines and labels as people need to estimate a value.
Give every chart a title and a short summary that state its main point, so people know what it shows before reading the detail.
Keep the data the most prominent layer; axes, labels and text stay quieter and support it.
In a narrow layout give the plot the full width and keep vertical-axis labels short, moving units into the title.
Show the essential information without interaction; interaction may reveal extra detail only.
When marks are too small to hit, make the whole plot area the target and let people scrub across it.
Let keyboard and switch users move through the data in a logical order, stepping through groups when the set is large.
Signal changes to marks or axes in a way other than animation, so screen-reader users and people with reduced motion notice them.
Never use color as the only way to tell series apart; add shape, pattern or a direct label.
Put a small gap between adjacent colored segments, such as the parts of a stacked bar.

rules.section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
rules.rule: Give assistive technology an overview of the chart: its type, what each axis measures and its range; on Apple platforms, use Audio Graphs.

rules.section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
rules.rule: Label each important mark, or each group of marks, with its context and the actual value, in plain unambiguous words; describe what a series means, not its color.

rules.section: Enhancing the accessibility of a chart
rules.rule: Hide the visible axis and tick labels from screen readers when the mark labels and overview already carry that information.
On watchOS, show a chart people can read at a glance with at most simple interactions; keep deep exploration for larger devices.

properties.ios: Chart with BarMark, LineMark or PointMark (Swift Charts)
properties.android: custom drawing in Canvas (Material 3 has no chart component)
properties.web: chart pages (bar, line, …) drawn with tokens
Grid line and Data label patterns
role="img" with aria-label plus a text summary or data table

ios-components|Image views.summary: A view that shows a single image, or an animated sequence of images, and is normally not interactive.

rules.rule: Use an image view only to display an image; when an image must act, put it in a button rather than adding tap handling to the image.
Show icons as symbols or interface icons, not as image views, so they take the theme and accent colors.
When text sits on an image, make sure it keeps enough contrast, using a scrim, a background layer or a shadow.
Give every frame of an animated sequence the same size, and prescale images to the view where you can.
On macOS, use an image well when people need to paste, drag or clear the image, and an image button when it must be clickable.
On tvOS, use layered images where depth adds to the focus effect.
On visionOS, image views can show 2D, stereoscopic and spatial images; follow the visionOS image guidance for each kind.
On watchOS, prefer SwiftUI animation; animate an image sequence only when needed.

properties.web: object-fit through the Preview aspect prop

properties.ios: Image(_:label:) or accessibilityLabel(_:) / isAccessibilityElement and accessibilityLabel

ios-components|Text views.summary: A scrolling region for long, rich or editable text; short text belongs in a label or a text field.

rules.rule: Use a text view for text that is long, editable or specially formatted; use a label for short read-only text and a text field for a short value.
Keep text legible: support Dynamic Type and test with larger text and bold text turned on.
Let people select and copy useful read-only text such as error codes, serial numbers or addresses.
On iOS and iPadOS, show the keyboard that fits the content being edited.
On tvOS, use a text view only to display text; take text input with a text field.

properties.ios: TextEditor (editable) or Text (read only) / UITextView isEditable
properties.android: TextField or OutlinedTextField with minLines and maxLines

ios-components|Web views.summary: An embedded view that renders web content, such as an HTML message or a short page, inside the app.

rules.rule: When people may follow links to several pages, turn on back and forward navigation and show controls for it.
Use a web view to show content briefly in context, never to build a general web browser; send full browsing to the system browser.
Plan another presentation on tvOS and watchOS, which have no web view.

ios-components|Boxes.summary: A visually bounded area, with a border or a background and an optional title, that groups related content.

rules.rule: Keep a box clearly smaller than the view that holds it; a box that nearly fills the screen no longer reads as a group.
Do not nest boxes to show subgroups; use spacing and alignment inside the box instead.
Add a title only when it clarifies how the contents relate; it also helps screen-reader users know what is inside.
Write the title as a short phrase in sentence case with no ending punctuation, except the colon a macOS settings pane uses.
On iOS and iPadOS, rely on the system secondary and tertiary backgrounds for the box fill.
On macOS, the title sits above the box.

ios-components|Collections.summary: An ordered set of items, usually images, shown in a row or a grid that people can scroll, select and edit.

rules.rule: Use the standard row or grid layout; avoid custom layouts that confuse people or draw attention to themselves.
Show mostly textual content in a list or table instead of a collection.
Leave enough room around items that focus and hover effects stay visible and items never overlap.
Add custom gestures only when the app needs them, on top of the standard select, edit and scroll interactions.
Animate inserting, deleting and reordering items so people can follow the change.
On iOS and iPadOS, do not change a collection's layout while people are using it unless they asked for the change.

properties.ios: LazyVGrid / LazyHGrid / UICollectionView with a layout
List selection or custom / UICollectionView allowsSelection, allowsMultipleSelection
properties.android: custom selected state on the item

ios-components|Column views.summary: A macOS browser that shows a hierarchy as side-by-side columns, one level per column, also called Miller columns.

rules.rule: Use a column view for a deep hierarchy that people move up and down often and that does not need sorting; use a table when it does.
Show the top level of the hierarchy in the first column.
When the selected item has no children, use the next column for a preview or details of it.
Let people resize columns so long names can be read.
Column views exist only on macOS; on other platforms show the hierarchy with a split view or a navigation stack.

ios-components|Disclosure controls.summary: A control that shows or hides related content: a disclosure triangle for a section or list, a disclosure button for a control's extra options.

rules.rule: Keep the most used options visible and put advanced ones behind a disclosure control, collapsed by default.
Give a disclosure triangle a label that names what it reveals.
Point the indicator toward the leading edge when collapsed and down when expanded, and resize the view to fit the content.
Place a disclosure button next to the content it reveals so the relationship is obvious.
Use at most one disclosure button in a view.
On iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, build disclosure with DisclosureGroup.

properties.android: Row with Text and an expand IconButton

ios-components|Labels.summary: Short, read-only text that names or explains something, in buttons, list rows, menus and views.

rules.rule: Use a label for a small amount of read-only text; use a text field when it must be edited and a text view when it is long.
Prefer the system font and keep custom styles legible at every Dynamic Type size.
Show importance with the system label colors (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary) rather than custom colors.
Let people select and copy useful label text such as an error message, a location or an address.
On macOS, show read-only text with a text field whose editing is turned off.
On watchOS, use the system date and timer text, which fits and updates itself, including in complications.

properties.web: ListItem icon or the icon prop of the owning component

ios-components|Lists and tables.summary: Rows of data in one or more columns, grouped or hierarchical, that people can scan, select, edit and reorder.

rules.rule: Use a list or table for text-first content; use a collection for many images or items of very different sizes.
Let people edit a list where it makes sense; reordering alone is often worth offering.
Show selection clearly: keep the selected row highlighted in a navigation list, and mark chosen options with a checkmark.
Keep row text short; for long items list the titles and open the content in a detail view.
When text must be shortened, consider truncating in the middle so both its start and end stay recognizable.
Give each column of a multicolumn table a short noun heading with no ending punctuation; give a single-column list a header or label for context.
Choose the list and row style that fits the data and the platform, such as grouped sections or a leading image with a label.
On iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, use a disclosure indicator to drill into a row and an info button only to show more about it.
On iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, do not add a section index to a list whose rows have trailing controls.
On macOS, sort by a column when its heading is clicked and reverse on a second click; let people resize columns; consider alternating row colors in wide tables; use an outline view for hierarchy.
On tvOS, check that images next to a row still look right as the focused row grows and rounds its corners.
On watchOS, keep lists short with the most relevant items first and a way to see more, and keep detail views short enough to page between.

ios-components|Lockups.summary: A tvOS unit that joins an image or control with a header and footer, which grow together when the lockup takes focus.

rules.rule: Leave enough space between lockups that a focused one can grow without covering or pushing its neighbors.
Give every lockup in a row or group the same size.
Use a card lockup for ratings and reviews of a media item.
Let caption buttons tilt with the swipe direction when focused, matching their arrangement in a row, column or grid.
Show a photo of the person in a monogram when one exists; initials are the fallback.
Size each poster to its content; the title and subtitle appear only when it has focus.
Lockups exist only on tvOS.

ios-components|Outline views.summary: A macOS table whose first column shows a hierarchy with disclosure triangles, with optional columns for attributes.

rules.rule: Use an outline view for hierarchical text data, often in the leading pane of a split view; use a table when the data is flat.
Show the hierarchy in the first column only; other columns hold attributes of each row.
Give every column of a multicolumn outline view a short noun heading without punctuation.
Let people sort by clicking a heading, sorting within each level of the hierarchy, and resize columns.
Make expanding and collapsing easy, with a modifier to expand a whole branch, and remember what people expanded.
Let people edit cells where that makes sense, and keep single click and double click behaviors distinct.
Consider middle truncation for long cell text and a search field for long outlines.
Outline views exist only on macOS; elsewhere show hierarchy with nested lists or disclosure groups.

properties.web: Tree nodes, or DataTable with options.dataTree

ios-components|Split views.summary: Two or three side-by-side panes that show levels of a hierarchy at once, such as a sidebar, a list and a detail.

Let people drag content between panes when that helps them move it through the hierarchy.
On iPhone, use a split view only in a regular-width environment; in compact width it collapses to one pane at a time.
On iPadOS, design the split view for narrow, intermediate and wide windows, and keep navigation between panes logical at each width.

Label every tab with a short noun or noun phrase that predicts its pane, in title case.

Place the tabs on the top edge of the content and inset the tab view from the window edges; hide the tabs only when the app switches panes itself.

Title each custom action with a short verb phrase, without the company or product name.
Exclude system activities that make no sense in the app, and show only custom ones that fit the current content.
Open the share sheet from the standard Share button, not from a custom control.
Keep a share or action extension short and familiar: prefer the system composer, show the app's name and style, and finish in a few steps.

Give every custom button a visible pressed state.
Style the most likely action as prominent, and allow at most a couple of prominent buttons in one view.
Mark the preferred option with a stronger style, not a larger size; buttons offered as a set share one size.
Avoid tinting button labels with the same color as bright content behind them; keep the default monochrome look there.

On macOS, end a push button's title with an ellipsis when it opens another window or view for more input.
On macOS, keep square, help and image buttons inside views, never in the toolbar or window frame, and use at most one help button per window.

ios-components|Context menus.summary: A menu of the most relevant actions for an item, opened by touch and hold, a secondary click or Control-click.

Offer context menus consistently across the app, and make every command in them available in the main interface too.
Keep submenus to one level and give each a title that predicts its contents.
Hide commands that do not apply instead of dimming them (on macOS, Cut, Copy and Paste may stay dimmed).
Put the most used items nearest the point where the menu opens, and use no more than about three separated groups.
Show keyboard shortcuts in the main menus, not in context menus.
On iOS, iPadOS and visionOS, place destructive items last and mark them as destructive.
Give each item a short clear label and a familiar icon; add a menu title only when it clarifies the effect, such as how many items are selected.

ios-components|Dock menus.summary: The macOS menu that appears on an app's Dock icon, with system items and a few custom ones.

rules.rule: Label and group Dock menu items like any other menu.
Make every custom Dock menu command available elsewhere in the app too.
Add only high-value items, such as open windows and the actions most useful when the app is in the background.

ios-components|Edit menus.summary: The system menu of editing commands, such as Cut, Copy, Paste and Select, for the current selection.

rules.rule: Use the system edit menu instead of a custom copy of it.
Open it with the standard platform interactions, never a custom gesture.
Show only commands that apply now: no Copy without a selection, no Paste with nothing to paste.
Place custom commands next to related system commands, and add only a few.
Let people select and copy read-only content text, but not control labels.
Support undo and redo, since edit commands act without confirmation.
Avoid separate controls that repeat edit commands, and make the different kinds of deletion clear.
Label custom commands with a short verb or verb phrase.

ios-components|Home Screen quick actions.summary: Up to four shortcuts that appear when people touch and hold the app icon, each opening a key task directly.

rules.rule: Offer quick actions for compelling, frequent tasks; most apps should have at least one, and four is the limit.
Update dynamic quick actions only in ways people can predict.
Title each action with a short phrase that says what happens, adding a subtitle only for useful context; never include the app name.
Give each action a familiar monochrome symbol or interface icon; never an emoji.

ios-components|Menus.summary: A list of commands, options or states that opens from a control; the rules here apply to every kind of menu.

rules.rule: Label each item clearly and briefly, starting actions with a verb; drop articles such as a and the.
Use title-style capitalization in menu labels, as the platform does.
Dim unavailable items but keep the menu itself openable, so people can see what it offers.
End a label with an ellipsis when the command needs more input before it runs.
Use standard icons for common actions, add icons only where they help recognition, and give either all or none of the items in a group an icon.
List important and frequent items first, group related items with separators, and keep related commands together even when used less often.
Keep menus short; split a long menu or use a submenu, unless it lists the person's own items.
Use submenus sparingly, one level deep and about five items at most, named with the term their items share.
Keep a submenu openable even when all its items are unavailable, and never use indentation instead of a submenu.
For an on-off attribute use one item whose label shows the state (adding a verb if needed) or a checkmark, and offer one item that clears several toggles.
Let players navigate game menus with the platform's usual input, and keep text and targets large enough on every screen.
On iOS and iPadOS, use the small or medium layout only for a few closely related actions with recognizable symbols.
On visionOS, place a menu near the content it controls and prefer the subtle breakthrough effect.

ios-components|Ornaments.summary: A visionOS panel attached to the edge of a window that holds controls or information and moves with the window.

rules.rule: Use an ornament for frequent controls or information that should stay in one predictable place without cluttering the window.
Keep ornaments visible, hiding them only while people are immersed in content.
Limit the number of ornaments to keep the window balanced, and keep each no wider than its window.
Use borderless buttons on an ornament's glass background.
Use the system toolbar and tab bar, which become ornaments automatically, instead of building them as custom ornaments.
Ornaments exist only on visionOS.

ios-components|Pop-up buttons.summary: A button that opens a menu of mutually exclusive options and then shows the chosen one.

rules.rule: Use a pop-up button for a flat list of mutually exclusive options; use a pull-down button for actions, multiple selection or submenus.
Show a useful default that most people would choose when nothing is selected yet.
Make the options predictable before opening, with an introductory label or a label that states the effect.
Use a pop-up button where space is short and the options need not be visible all the time.
Add a Custom option for rarely needed choices instead of crowding the menu, with brief explanatory text if needed.
On iPadOS, inside a popover or a modal, a short fixed list of choices can live in a pop-up button rather than a row that pushes a new view.

ios-components|Pull-down buttons.summary: A button that opens a menu of commands related to its own action; choosing one runs it.

rules.rule: Use a pull-down button for commands that refine or redirect the button's action; use a pop-up button for a choice among options.
Do not hide a view's primary actions in a pull-down button.
List roughly three or more items; with one or two, use buttons or toggles, and avoid menus so long they slow people down.
Add a menu title only when it adds meaning.
Mark destructive items as destructive and ask people to confirm before running them.
Add an icon after an item's label only when it clarifies the item.

On iOS and iPadOS, use a More button for secondary items where space is short, weighing the space saved against discoverability.
