ios-components|The menu bar.summary: The bar of app menus at the top of the screen on macOS and iPadOS, listing every command the app offers.

rules.rule: Keep the standard menus in their standard order: the app menu, File, Edit, Format, View, app-specific menus, Window, Help.
Support the system menus and their order, and keep the same items present, disabling rather than hiding what does not apply.
Support the standard keyboard shortcuts for standard items; add custom shortcuts only when needed.
Use familiar icons for common actions and short, one-word menu titles.
Put items about the app as a whole in the app menu, with About first in its own group.
Use the File menu for document commands; rename or remove it when the app has no files.
Keep the Edit menu even in apps without documents, and decide whether Find belongs there or in File.
Include the Format menu only when the app edits formatted text.
Provide a View menu even for a single view option, and keep each Show or Hide title in step with the current state.
List every custom command in an app-specific menu, ordered from general to specialized and mirroring the app's hierarchy.
Provide a Window menu even with a single window, including Minimize and Zoom for keyboard users.
Keep Help last and use it to open the app's help.
Never make a dynamic item, revealed with a modifier key, the only way to do something; use it only in the menu bar and with a single modifier.
On iPadOS, make every function reachable in the interface too, since the menu bar is often hidden.
On iPadOS, use Settings in the app menu for the app's page in system Settings, list tabs in the View menu, and group items into submenus more often than on the Mac.
On macOS, open a menu (not a popover) from a menu bar extra, let people choose whether to show it, and never rely on it being visible.

ios-components|Toolbars.summary: A bar at the top or bottom of a view that holds its title, navigation controls and the actions for its content.

rules.rule: Choose toolbar items deliberately so each one can be told apart and reached, and decide which ones move to overflow as the view narrows.
Rely on the system overflow on macOS and iPadOS rather than adding one, and use a More menu only for actions that do not fit.
On iPadOS and macOS, let people customize the toolbar in apps with many items or long sessions.
Avoid custom toolbar backgrounds and tinted items; let the content set the color, and use the standard components and corner radii.
Hide toolbars for distraction-free work only in context, with a reliable way to bring them back.
Give each window a concise title (under about 15 characters) that names its content, never the app's name; leave it empty if it adds nothing.
Use the standard Back and Close buttons with their standard symbols, not text labels.
Make every item's meaning clear; prefer familiar borderless symbols, and text only where no symbol fits.
Show at most one primary action, in the prominent style, at the trailing end.
Place navigation and the title at the leading edge, common controls in the center, and important actions, search and More at the trailing edge.
Group items by function and frequency, in no more than about three groups, consistent across platforms.
Separate text-labeled actions from each other and from symbols with fixed space so they do not read as one control.
On iOS, keep only the essential actions in the toolbar, put the rest in a More menu, and use a large title on top-level views.
On iPadOS, consider combining the toolbar with a tab bar in the same row.
On macOS, make every toolbar command also available in the menu bar.
On visionOS, use the system toolbar at the bottom of the window, never a vertical one or a pull-down menu, and keep the window at least as wide as the toolbar.
On watchOS, place controls in the upper corners or across the foot of the screen, and keep one important secondary action in a scrolling toolbar button.

rules.rule: Place a path control inside the window's content area, never in a toolbar or status bar.
Pick the inline style when there is room to show the whole chain and the pop-up style when space is tight.
Use a path control on macOS only; on iOS, iPadOS and the web, show a location with a breadcrumb or the navigation stack instead.

ios-components|Search fields.summary: A text field for finding content by typing terms, with a search icon, a clear button and optional scopes or tokens to narrow the results.

rules.rule: Write placeholder text that names what can be searched, such as the content type or the scope.
Update results as the person types rather than waiting for a submit, when the data allows it.
Offer recent searches before typing starts and suggestions while typing.
Put the most relevant results first and group them by kind when that helps scanning.
Start with the broadest scope and let a scope bar narrow it to clearly separate categories.
Turn common filters into tokens inside the field, and surface the available tokens through suggestions so people discover them.

On iOS, choose the entry point by role: a search tab for an app-wide destination, a bottom toolbar field when search is a priority, a top bar button when bottom content matters, or an inline field above the list it filters.
On iOS, use the standard search tab when the landing page should invite browsing and the button style when people mostly want a quick lookup.
On iPad and Mac, place search at the trailing end of the toolbar, at the top of the sidebar when it filters the sidebar, or as its own sidebar item when it leads to a discovery area.
Focus the field on arrival in a dedicated search area, except on iPad with only the on-screen keyboard, where the keyboard would cover the view.
On tvOS, lean on suggestions and recent searches, since typing with a remote is slow.
On watchOS, expect text entry to take the full screen and return to the field only after Cancel or Search.

Let people choose and reorder the sidebar items they use most, where the app allows it.
Use disclosure groups to keep a long sidebar short, and keep group titles brief.
Show at most two levels of hierarchy; for deeper data add a content list between the sidebar and the detail.
Use familiar symbols for items, and give an icon a fixed color only when the color carries meaning.
Let people hide the sidebar with the gesture or command they know, but show it by default so it stays discoverable.
On iPhone and iPad, start with a tab bar and offer the sidebar-adaptable style only when there are more areas than the bar can hold.

ios-components|Tab bars.summary: A bar of labeled destinations for moving between an app's top-level sections, each keeping its own place.

rules.rule: Use tabs only to navigate; put actions on the current view in a toolbar.
Keep the tab bar on screen in every section; only a modal view may cover it.
Keep the number of tabs small enough that none spill into a More tab; move to a sidebar when the structure is larger.
Never disable or remove a tab when its content is missing; show the section and explain why it is empty.
Label every tab, with one word where possible, and pair it with a familiar symbol, preferably filled.
Badge a tab only for information that needs attention, so the badge keeps its weight.
Keep tab colors distinct from colorful content behind the bar, or use a monochrome bar.

On iPadOS, prefer the tab bar near the top, allow conversion to a sidebar for larger apps, and keep a customizable default at five tabs or fewer.

Accept extra keys, such as Return, for turning typed text into a token, beyond the default comma.
Delay token suggestions slightly when instant ones would distract people mid-typing.
Use a token field on macOS only; elsewhere use search tokens or a tag input.

ios-components|Action sheets.summary: A modal list of choices that appears in response to an action the person started, such as deleting or discarding.

rules.rule: Use an action sheet for choices about an action the person started, and an alert for an unexpected problem.
Show action sheets only when a choice is truly needed, since each one interrupts the task.
Keep the title to one line and add a message only when the title and context are not enough.
Include a Cancel button when the action could destroy data, placed at the bottom.
Give destructive choices the destructive style and put them at the top.
On iPhone and iPad, use an action sheet rather than a menu for choices that follow an action.
On iPhone and iPad, keep the list short enough that it never scrolls.
On watchOS, use no more than four buttons including Cancel.

ios-components|Alerts.summary: A modal message that interrupts to report something critical and asks for a decision about it.

rules.rule: Use an alert only for information that needs action now; show anything merely informative in context.
Skip alerts for common actions that can be undone; keep them for rare destructive actions that cannot.
Never open an alert at launch; show start-up problems in the screen instead.
Write a title that states what happened and why in two lines at most, never a bare code or the word Error.
Add body text only when it helps, keep the tone neutral and direct, and do not explain the buttons.
Add a text field only when the input is needed to resolve the situation.
Title buttons with one or two words that name the result, such as Delete or Reply; reserve OK for purely informational alerts and always use Cancel to cancel.
Place the preferred action last in a horizontal row or first in a vertical stack, with Cancel opposite it.
Mark a button destructive only when it does damage the person did not ask for, and pair any destructive choice with a Cancel button that is not the default.
Let Escape and the platform's cancel gestures dismiss the alert as Cancel.
On iPhone and iPad, keep alerts short so they do not scroll at large text sizes, and use an action sheet for choices about a chosen action.
On macOS, use the caution symbol only when data could be lost unexpectedly.
On visionOS, keep any accessory view at most 154 pt high with a 16 pt corner radius.

ios-components|Page controls.summary: A row of dots that shows how many pages a flat, ordered set has and which one is showing.

rules.rule: Use a page control only for an ordered, flat set of peer pages, never for hierarchy.
Center the control near the bottom of the view.
Keep the set to about ten pages; beyond that, use a grid or another layout people can jump around in.
Replace a dot with a simple symbol only to mark one special page, and use no more than two indicator images in total.
Leave indicator colors to the system so the current page keeps its contrast.
On iPhone and iPad, animate page changes for taps but not while scrubbing.
On iPhone and iPad, show the background always only when the control is the main navigation, and turn off scrubbing with the minimal background.
On tvOS, use page controls for full-screen pages without other controls competing for focus.
On watchOS, prefer vertical pages moved with the Digital Crown, each with one clear purpose and ideally one screen tall.

ios-components|Panels.summary: A macOS window that floats over the app's windows to hold controls or details for the current selection, such as an inspector.

rules.rule: Use a panel for quick controls or details tied to the selection, such as an inspector that updates as the selection changes.
Fill a panel with direct controls such as sliders and steppers rather than typing or multi-step selection.
Give the panel a short noun title, and use that title, without the word panel, in menus and help.
Bring all open panels forward when the app activates and hide them when it is inactive.
Leave panels out of the Window menu's document list and do not offer a minimize button.
Use the dark HUD style only in media-focused apps where a standard panel would hide content, keep it small with little color, and keep the same style across modes.
On iOS, iPadOS and the web, show the same supplementary content in a sheet, an inspector or a side panel instead.

ios-components|Popovers.summary: A short-lived view anchored to the control that opened it, for a little information or a few related actions.

rules.rule: Keep a popover to a small amount of content and a few related tasks.
Point the arrow at the element that opened it, and avoid covering that element or content needed alongside.
Close the popover on an outside tap or a choice; add Cancel or Done only when save-or-discard needs to be clear, and stay open while several choices are made.
Keep the person's work when a nonmodal popover closes itself; discard it only on an explicit Cancel.
Show one popover at a time, never one opened from another, and nothing on top of it except an alert.
Let one click close the open popover and open the next.
Size it to its content and animate any change in size.
Never use a popover for a warning; use an alert.
On compact widths, present the content as a sheet instead of a popover.
On macOS, consider letting people drag a popover off into a panel that looks almost the same.

ios-components|Scroll views.summary: A region that lets people move content larger than its bounds, showing an indicator of position while scrolling.

rules.rule: Support the standard scrolling gestures and keys, with the elastic edge behavior people expect.
Make overflow obvious, for example by letting content run partly past the edge.
Never nest scroll views that scroll in the same direction; a horizontal row inside a vertical page is fine.
Offer paging when content comes in screen-sized units, keeping a little overlap for context.
Scroll automatically only to bring a new selection, the insertion point or a drag into view, and only as far as needed.
When zoom is supported, set sensible minimum and maximum scales.
Use the automatic edge effect, only where content scrolls under floating bars, and only one per view, with matching heights across panes.
On iPhone and iPad, pair paged scrolling with a page control and hide the scroll indicator on that axis.
On macOS, use small scroll bars in a crowded panel only together with small controls throughout.
On visionOS, leave margin for the indicator and add Look to Scroll to reading and browsing views consistently, but not to dense control areas.
On watchOS, prefer vertical scrolling with the Digital Crown.

properties.web: bars shown on hover or focus (system/scrolling.css)

ios-components|Sheets.summary: A view that slides over the current screen for a short, self-contained task, then returns people to where they were.

rules.rule: Use Cancel to leave without saving, Done to finish or save, and Back only to step back in a flow, never to close the sheet.
Move long or complex flows to a full-screen view or a separate window instead of a sheet.
Show one sheet at a time; close the first before opening another.
Pair Done with Cancel or with Back, and never show all three together.
Use a nonmodal presentation when the content adjusts the parent view while people keep working in it.
On iPhone and iPad, put Cancel on the leading edge of the sheet's top bar and Done on the trailing edge.
On iPhone, add the medium detent when the first half of the content is useful on its own, and show a grabber whenever the sheet resizes.
Allow swipe down to dismiss, and confirm with an action sheet first when there are unsaved changes.
On iPad, prefer the page or form sheet styles.
On macOS, open sheets at a size that fits their content, let people use other windows meanwhile, and use a panel for repeated input and review.
On visionOS, center the sheet in view rather than raising it from the window's bottom, and keep it smaller than its window.
On watchOS, use a sheet only for brief, occasional tasks that need custom content, never for navigation.

ios-components|Windows.summary: The frame that holds an app's views on iPadOS, macOS and visionOS, which people open, resize, move and close.

rules.rule: Make every window adapt smoothly to any size it can take.
Open a new window only when seeing two things at once helps, and offer it as a command rather than the default.
Use the system's window frames and controls; never draw imitations.
Call it a window in interface text, never a scene or another term.
On iPadOS, move leading toolbar items inward when the window controls appear, so they are not covered.
On iPadOS, consider a gesture such as pinch to open an item in its own window.
On macOS, keep the system appearances for main, key and inactive windows in any custom window.
On macOS, use a bottom bar only for a little status about the window, and never for critical content.
On visionOS, keep the glass background, choose an initial size and shape that fit the content with little empty space, and set minimum and maximum sizes.
On visionOS, use a volume rather than a window for deep 3D content, and keep 2D content in it readable from every angle.

ios-components|Color wells.summary: A control that shows the current color and opens a color picker to change it.

rules.rule: Use the system color picker unless the app truly needs its own, so people keep their saved colors and a familiar layout.
On macOS, highlight the well while its picker is open, update it as soon as a color is chosen, and support dragging colors between wells.
Do not plan on a color well for tvOS or watchOS, where the control is not available.

ios-components|Combo boxes.summary: A macOS text field joined to a list button, so people can type their own value or pick a suggested one.

rules.rule: Prefill the field with a meaningful value from the list, not necessarily the first.
Introduce the box with a label that says what kind of value it takes.
List the most likely choices while still accepting custom entries.
Keep list items no wider than the field, so nothing is truncated.
On iOS and iPadOS, use a text field with suggestions or a picker instead, since combo boxes are macOS only.

ios-components|Digit entry views.summary: A tvOS full-screen prompt for a short run of digits, such as a PIN, entered on a digit keyboard.

rules.rule: Mask the digits whenever the value is sensitive.
Give the view a title and prompt that say why the digits are needed.
On iOS and the web, use a number field or a code input with the numeric keyboard instead, since digit entry views are tvOS only.

ios-components|Image wells.summary: A macOS image view that people can edit by dropping, pasting, copying or deleting an image.
