ios-components|Pickers.summary: A control that shows one or more scrolling lists of values, such as dates or options, for people to choose from.

rules.rule: Use a picker for medium to long lists; a short list fits a pull-down button and a very long one fits a list or table.
Order values predictably, for example alphabetically, so people can guess the hidden ones.
Show the picker next to the value being edited, in place or in a popover, rather than on a new screen.
Use a coarser minute interval that divides evenly into 60 when exact minutes are not needed.
On iPhone and iPad, choose the date picker style and mode that fit the task, and use the compact style when space is tight.
On macOS, use the textual date picker for exact entry in tight space and the graphical one for browsing days or picking a range.
On tvOS, build pickers with SwiftUI.
On watchOS, let people move through values with the Digital Crown, and show long lists behind a button.

properties.web: Date picker, Time picker or Date-time picker

properties.ios: DatePicker in: range / UIDatePicker minimumDate and maximumDate

ios-components|Segmented controls.summary: A row of joined segments, each acting as a button, for choosing among a few closely related options or views.

rules.rule: Use a segmented control for closely related choices that change an object, a state or a view.
Keep one behavior per control: either every segment shows a selection or every segment performs an action.
Limit the control to about five segments on iPhone and about seven on wider layouts.
Keep segments equal in width.
Use text or icons in a control, not a mix, with content of similar size in every segment.
Label segments with short nouns in title case; a text-labeled control needs no introduction.
On iPhone and iPad, use it to switch between related subviews, and a tab bar for separate app sections.
On macOS, give icon segments a label or tooltip, and use a tab view rather than a segmented control to switch the main window area.
On tvOS, keep other focusable items away from the control, since segments select on focus.
On visionOS, supply descriptive text for icon segments, shown as a tooltip when people look at them.

ios-components|Sliders.summary: A track with a thumb that people drag to set a value between a minimum and a maximum.

rules.rule: Customize the track, thumb or end icons only when it explains what the slider controls.
Put the minimum at the leading end of a horizontal slider and at the bottom of a vertical one.
Add a number field, and a stepper where whole steps help, when the range is wide or exact values matter.
On iPhone and iPad, use the system volume view for audio volume, not a slider.
On macOS, show results live as the value changes, use tick marks with sparse labels for precision, and introduce the slider with a label.
On macOS, use a linear slider for a fixed range and a circular one for values that wrap around, such as rotation.
On visionOS, prefer horizontal sliders.
On watchOS, replace the default plus and minus with custom symbols when they explain the value better.

properties.ios: Slider in: bounds / UISlider minimumValue and maximumValue
Slider step / custom rounding in UISlider
Slider minimumValueLabel and maximumValueLabel / UISlider minimumValueImage and maximumValueImage

ios-components|Steppers.summary: A pair of minus and plus buttons that change a value by a fixed step, shown next to the value it changes.

rules.rule: Show the value the stepper changes right next to it, since the stepper itself shows none.
Pair the stepper with an editable number field when values can vary widely.
On macOS, consider Shift-click for a larger step when the range is big.
Do not plan on a stepper for tvOS or watchOS, where the control is not available.

properties.android: custom view: two IconButtons around the value

properties.ios: Stepper in: bounds / UIStepper minimumValue and maximumValue

ios-components|Toggles.summary: A control for choosing between two opposite states, such as on and off, shown as a switch, a checkbox or a toggling button.

rules.rule: Use a toggle only for two opposite states; use a pop-up or another control for picking from a list.
Make clear what the toggle controls, through its row, a label or its icon.
Show the state through shape or content as well as color, never by color alone.
On iPhone and iPad, use a switch only in a list row, and a button that toggles elsewhere.
On iPhone and iPad, change the switch color only to the app accent, keeping enough contrast with the off state.
On macOS, put switches, checkboxes and radio buttons in the content of the window, not in its toolbar or status bar.
On macOS, use a switch for an important setting or one that controls a group, mini switches for single rows in a grouped form, and do not swap existing checkboxes for switches.
On macOS, use checkboxes, aligned and indented, for a hierarchy of settings, and show the mixed state when the children differ.
On macOS, use radio buttons for two to about five mutually exclusive options; switch to a pop-up for more, and to a checkbox for a single on or off setting.
On macOS, space horizontal radio buttons evenly, using the width of the longest label.

ios-components|Virtual keyboards.summary: The on-screen keyboard that devices without a hardware keyboard show for text entry, with layouts tuned to the content.

rules.rule: Request the keyboard that matches the content, and declare the content type so the system can suggest and correct well.
Set the Return key to the action it performs, such as Search, Go or Next.
Replace the system keyboard with a custom input view only when it clearly makes the task easier, and play the standard key click.
Ship a systemwide custom keyboard only for input the system cannot provide, with an obvious way to switch keyboards.
Do not repeat system keys such as Globe or Dictation, and teach the keyboard in the app rather than inside the keyboard.
On iPhone and iPad, follow the keyboard layout guide so the focused field and key controls stay visible above the keyboard.
On iPhone and iPad, put only task-related controls in a bar above the keyboard, using a standard toolbar so it matches the system.
On visionOS, do not reserve layout space for the keyboard; it appears in its own movable window.
On watchOS, set the text content type, since the keyboard type cannot be changed and input may come from dictation or Scribble.
On tvOS, expect the linear keyboard with the remote and the digit keyboard for digit entry.

properties.web: inputmode none with an in-page keypad

ios-components|Activity rings.summary: The system's Move, Exercise and Stand rings, shown in a health or fitness app to report one person's progress toward their daily activity goals.

rules.rule: Show the rings only where activity progress belongs to the task, such as a live workout screen or a workout summary.
Use the rings for Move, Exercise and Stand data alone; never repurpose them for other data or draw that data in a look-alike ring.
Show one person's progress per element and identify that person with a name, photo or avatar.

Keep the rings exactly as the system draws them: original colors, a black background that stays visible around the outer ring, no effects, and the surrounding layout adapting to the rings rather than the reverse.
Color a label or value tied to a ring with that ring's own color.
Keep an empty margin around the rings at least as wide as the gap between rings, and let nothing overlap it.
Separate any other ring-shaped graphic from the Activity rings with spacing, a divider, a label, color or size.
Do not use the rings in notifications, as decoration, in an app icon or in marketing, and do not resend progress updates the system already delivers.
On iOS, expect a single Move ring when no Apple Watch is paired and three rings when one is, and design history views that can show both forms.

ios-components|Gauges.summary: A circular or linear display of one numeric value inside a known range, optionally with labels for the range ends and a color spectrum.

rules.rule: Pick the standard style to mark the value with an indicator and the capacity style to fill the path up to the value; use the accessory variant where the gauge should match watch complications or Lock Screen widgets.
Label the current value and both ends of the range with short text, because assistive technologies read those labels aloud.
Use a gradient fill when it reinforces what the range means, such as warm to cool for temperature.
On macOS, use the continuous capacity style for a large range, since discrete segments become too small to read.
On macOS, change the fill color at meaningful thresholds such as very low or very high, either for the whole indicator or as tiers.

properties.android: LinearProgressIndicator progress (custom view for a true gauge)

properties.ios: tint(_:) with a Gradient / NSLevelIndicator warningValue, criticalValue, fillColor

ios-components|Progress indicators.summary: A bar or spinner that shows work is under way, and how far along it is when the length is known.

rules.rule: Show determinate progress whenever the amount of work is known, and switch from indeterminate to determinate as soon as it becomes known.
Report progress honestly and at an even pace; never race to near-complete and then stall.
Keep the indicator moving while work continues; if the work stalls, say what went wrong and what the person can do.
Do not change a spinner into a bar or a bar into a spinner during the same task.
Add a short, specific description of the task when it helps; skip generic words such as loading.
Place progress in the same spot every time so people know where to look.
Offer Cancel when stopping is safe, add Pause when stopping would lose work, and confirm before a cancel that throws progress away.
On iOS and iPadOS, refresh content automatically on a schedule and treat pull to refresh as an extra, not the only way to stay current.
Give a refresh control a title only when it tells something useful, such as when content last updated, never how to refresh.
On macOS, use an unlabeled spinner for background work or tight spaces such as inside a field or next to a button.
On watchOS, set a tint when the default white indicator does not suit the screen.

ios-components|Rating indicators.summary: A row of evenly spaced symbols, stars by default, that shows a whole-number rank.

rules.rule: Let people change a rating in place, right in the list, without opening a separate edit screen.
Keep the star unless another symbol is unmistakably a rating; an unfamiliar symbol hides the meaning.
Treat the rating indicator as a macOS control; on other platforms build the same behavior from standard controls.

ios-components|App Shortcuts.summary: Ready-made actions an app hands to Siri, Spotlight, the Shortcuts app and the Action button, available from the moment it is installed.

rules.rule: Adopt the system's app schemas for common kinds of functionality, and keep App Shortcuts for what is unique to your app.
Offer shortcuts for the most frequent and important tasks, ideally ones people finish without leaving where they are.
Allow at most one optional parameter, with a small set of familiar values people can recall without seeing a list.
When an optional value is missing, ask for it and suggest a likely default such as the last one used, with a few alternatives.
Keep spoken phrases simple enough to say in one breath; ask for further detail in a follow-up step.
Tell people a shortcut exists with an occasional in-app tip when they do the matching task.
Put every critical detail in the spoken dialogue, since the answer may arrive on a device with no screen; use a snippet for static results and a Live Activity for something that changes over time.
Write short, memorable invocation phrases that include the app name, plus natural variants.
Write App Shortcuts and Shortcuts in title case with Shortcuts plural, and a single shortcut in lowercase.
On iOS and iPadOS, list shortcuts most useful first, since that order sets their first appearance in Spotlight and Shortcuts.
On macOS, expose actions through App Intents so people can build their own shortcuts, since App Shortcuts are not offered there.

ios-components|Complications.summary: A small, always-current piece of an app's data shown on an Apple Watch face, opening the app when tapped.

rules.rule: Show live, glanceable data people care about; a static launcher alone earns little space on the face.
Support every complication family you can, falling back to an app image where you have no useful data for a family.
Offer several complications per family, each opening its own relevant place in the app.
Let people hide sensitive data, because an always-on face can be seen by others.
Schedule timeline entries for the moments the data matters, since updates and stored entries are limited.
Pick a closed gauge for a share of a whole, an open gauge for an arbitrary range, and a segmented gauge for fast-changing values.
Make every complication work in tinted mode: never rely on color alone, and supply a tinted image where desaturation spoils the full-color one.
Draw lines at least two points wide so they read on a moving wrist.
Provide static placeholder images for every complication you support.
Design circular images for the system's circular mask, and use the extra-large circular layouts for oversized content on the X-Large face.
Use the rectangular layout for charts and detail over time, and tune it for the Smart Stack with a meaningful background and relevance hints.
Use legacy templates only to support watch faces from before watchOS 9, sizing images to each template's published dimensions.

ios-components|Controls.summary: A system button or toggle from an app, placed in Control Center, on the Lock Screen or on the Action button for quick access.

rules.rule: Give every control a symbol, a title and, where it has a state, a value; the symbol must stand alone because some placements show nothing else.
Offer controls for actions that pay off without opening the app, such as starting a Live Activity.
Keep a control's state current after a tap, when an action finishes and from remote updates, including while an action is in progress.
Choose a symbol that suggests the action, with separate on and off symbols for a toggle, and animate changes of state.
Pick a brand tint that the system can apply to the on state and in the Dynamic Island.
Ask for any needed configuration when the control is first added, and allow changing it later.
Write verb-led hint text for the Action button, and placeholder text for any title or value that varies.
Redact private titles and values on a locked device, and require unlocking for actions that affect security.

rules.section: Camera experiences on a locked device
rules.rule: Reuse the app's own camera interface for the locked-device capture experience, require unlocking for anything beyond capture, and explain how to add the control.

ios-components|Live Activities.summary: A glanceable, updating view of a task or event with a clear start and end, shown on the Lock Screen, in the Dynamic Island and on other devices while it runs.

rules.rule: Design every presentation the system can choose: compact, minimal, expanded and Lock Screen, which it also reuses for StandBy, Apple Watch and CarPlay.
Use a Live Activity only for a bounded task or event that lasts no more than about eight hours.
Show only the few facts people need at a glance about the task, never ads or promotions; leave detail to the app.
Keep private details off a surface others can see: show a neutral summary or redact, and let people opt in to sensitive content.
Match the app's look in both light and dark appearances, show a logo mark without a container rather than the full app icon, and use medium or heavier text that reads at a glance.
Use even margins concentric with the rounded outer shape, keep content off the edges, and let the height grow or shrink with the amount of content.

Express the brand with bold foreground color on the black Dynamic Island, tint the key line to match, and check contrast for any custom Lock Screen background, including on a dimmed Always-On display.

rules.section: Adding transitions and animating content updates
rules.rule: Animate updates to draw attention to what changed, moving existing elements to new positions rather than removing and re-adding them, and avoid overlaps during the move.
Open the app at the related detail on tap, and add at most one essential button or toggle tied directly to the activity.

rules.section: Starting, updating, and ending a Live Activity
rules.rule: Start activities when people expect them, let them turn one off from the app, update only when content changes, and alert only for updates people must not miss.

rules.section: Starting, updating, and ending a Live Activity
rules.rule: End the activity as soon as the task ends, with a dismissal delay that suits it, often 15 to 30 minutes for a summary.

rules.section: Starting, updating, and ending a Live Activity
rules.rule: Track related events in one rotating Live Activity rather than several, and offer an App Shortcut that starts it.
In the compact presentation, make the two halves around the camera read as one balanced item, keep them narrow and snug to the camera, and link both to the same screen.
In the minimal presentation, show live data rather than just a logo while staying recognizable.
Keep elements in the same relative places when the activity expands, and wrap content tightly around the camera.

On the Lock Screen, design a layout of its own rather than a copy of a notification, use the standard 14-point margin, and check colors and the generated dismiss button on personalized wallpapers and in Dark Mode.
In StandBy, check assets at double scale, prefer the default background, keep standard margins and verify contrast under the red Night Mode tint.
Design for CarPlay and Apple Watch together, prefer timely content over controls because CarPlay disables them, and add a custom layout when larger text helps.
On watchOS, consider a custom Smart Stack layout that shows progress or key updates, leaving out buttons if the activity is likely to be watched while driving.

ios-components|Notifications.summary: A short, timely message from an app that people allowed to reach them as a banner, a Notification Center item or a badge.

rules.rule: Use the communication style, with the sender's picture and name, only for direct communication such as calls and messages.
Send short, useful notifications, and never repeat one about the same thing because it was not answered.
Do not use a notification to tell people to go and do something in the app; offer an action instead, or nothing.
Report errors in an alert, not a notification.
While the app is in front, show new information quietly in place, for example by updating a count or inserting the new item.
Leave out sensitive or personal details, since others may see the screen.
Use a brief title-case title without end punctuation that adds context, and let the system show the app name when only a generic title is possible.
Write the body in full sentences with sentence case and punctuation, do not truncate it yourself, and omit the app name and icon.
Provide neutral fallback text for when previews are hidden, and treat sound as a supplement that never carries the message alone.
Offer up to four time-saving actions with short title-case labels and a simple icon, none that merely opens the app.
Prefer actions that cannot destroy anything, and give enough context for any that can.
Use the app badge only for the count of unread notifications, keep it current, and never imitate a badge with a custom graphic.
Never rely on the badge alone for anything important, since people can turn badges off.
On watchOS, keep the short look discreet and never the only carrier of critical news, and provide a static long look with a dynamic one where possible.
On watchOS, put the most used nondestructive action first, because double tap triggers it.

ios-components|Snippets.summary: A compact view that shows the result of an action run from Siri, Spotlight or Shortcuts, or asks people to confirm it first.

rules.rule: Build a snippet from spoken dialogue, a custom view and the system buttons: Cancel and a primary button for confirmation, Done for a result.
Keep content legible on the system background in light and dark appearances, with consistent margins.
Keep the custom view within the 400-point height limit at every text size, and link to the app for more detail.
Label the confirm button with the specific action, such as Order, rather than OK or Continue.
Make the view explain itself without the dialogue text, which is meant for listening.

ios-components|Status bars.summary: The system strip along the top edge that shows the time, connection and battery.

rules.rule: Keep the status bar readable over content and never let controls sit beneath it; prefer a scroll edge effect that blurs content behind it.
Hide the status bar only for a while, during full-screen media.
Never hide it for good, and bring it back with a simple, discoverable gesture such as a tap.

ios-components|Top Shelf.summary: The area above the Apple TV Dock where an app in the top row features its content, ideally as full-screen dynamic previews.

rules.rule: Take people straight into content, with a primary button for playback and a More Info button for details.
Feature new and personalized content, such as new episodes or a place to resume, not things already watched or bought.
Leave out ads and prices; show a price only after someone shows interest.
Prefer dynamic full-screen content, and always supply at least one static fallback image that does not look interactive.
Give each carousel item a short title and, if useful, a brief subtitle.
In the details carousel, title the content that is playing and add the summary and metadata that help people choose.
Fill a sectioned row at least to the full screen width, include at least one label, and remember mixed image sizes scale to the tallest.
For scrolling banners, use three to eight images, put any text inside the image and repeat it in the accessibility label.

ios-components|Watch faces.summary: The Apple Watch home view people pick and fill with complications; apps can offer shareable, preconfigured faces.

rules.rule: Offer shareable watch faces that showcase several of your complications as a ready-made setup.
Show a preview of every face you share so people can see its value before adding it.
Cover every Apple Watch model by offering a comparable face for older devices, and label which devices each face supports.
When a chosen face is incompatible, offer a compatible alternative right away instead of an error.

ios-components|Widgets.summary: A glanceable view of an app's most useful, regularly refreshed content, with a few direct actions, placed on the Home Screen, Lock Screen, desktop, Smart Stack or in a room.

rules.rule: Decide early which sizes, contexts and rendering modes the widget supports, and design for each rather than relying only on the defaults.
Make the widget work in every appearance it can take: full color, tinted, clear and monochrome.
Build each widget around one simple idea tied to the app's main purpose, showing content that changes during the day and linking deep into the app.
Offer more sizes only when each adds real information or actions; never stretch a small layout to fill a big one.
Balance density so the essentials read at a glance and detail rewards a longer look.
Use brand color and type lightly, adding at most a small logo in the top trailing corner when content comes from several sources.
Do not copy the widget's look inside the app, and say when signing in unlocks more.
Refresh at a rate that matches the data, let the system update dates and times, show when data was last updated if needed, and animate updates for no more than two seconds.
Keep actions few and directly related, size targets for confident taps, and open the app at the exact related place.
Use the standard 16-point margin, or 11 points for tight groupings, and match inner corner radii to the widget's corners.
Use real text at 11 points or larger, never text baked into images, and prefer the system font and SF Symbols.
Never let color alone carry meaning, and keep full-color images for media such as album art.
Support light and dark appearances, preferably with semantic system colors.
Split the widget's content into the part that takes the accent tint and the rest, so the accented appearance can color each.
For the vibrant mode, draw content fully opaque in grayscale, lighter for primary and darker for secondary, and check contrast.
Show a realistic gallery preview, a placeholder of simple shapes while data loads, and one verb-led description for all sizes grouped together.

On iOS and iPadOS, treat Lock Screen widgets like complications, keep them legible on the dimmed Always-On display, drop backgrounds in StandBy and CarPlay, and use Live Activities for real-time updates.
On visionOS, design for the room: choose sizes, mounting and treatment styles that fit where people place the widget, simplify the layout at a distance, and test every tint palette and light level.
On watchOS, use a background color that carries meaning and provide relevance information so the Smart Stack can surface the widget.

ios-inputs|Action button.summary: A hardware button on supported iPhone and Apple Watch models that people assign to one frequently used function, such as an app's App Shortcut.

rules.rule: Offer a small set of essential actions for the button, and not one that just opens the app, since the system already covers that.
Label each action in title case with a present-tense verb first, no articles or prepositions, and three words at most.
Leave setup guidance to the system rather than repeating it inside the app.
On iOS, let an action finish in place, for example with a snippet or a Live Activity, without launching the app.
On watchOS, give later presses one simple secondary function that advances the first, such as marking a segment, and keep stopping a task in the interface.
On watchOS, pause the current activity when the Action and side buttons are pressed together, unless pausing would be unsafe, as during a dive.

ios-inputs|Apple Pencil and Scribble.summary: Precise stylus input on iPad for drawing, writing and marking up, with Scribble turning handwriting into text in any text field.

rules.rule: Support what people naturally try with a real pen, such as writing in margins, and let every control respond to the pencil as well as to a finger.
Make a mark the moment the pencil touches the screen, with no mode switch or button first.
Use pressure, tilt and orientation to shape strokes, mapping pressure to continuous properties such as opacity or width.
Keep feedback directly under the tip, and place controls where neither a left nor a right hand covers them, or let people move them.
Use hover only to preview the mark the tool will make, at a mid-range value and without changing with height, and never to trigger an action.
Show hover previews for the pencil only, not for a pointer, and use hover to offer tools near where people are marking.
Honor the system double-tap setting, make any custom behavior opt-in with a visible mode, and never use double tap to change content.
Treat squeeze as one quick, discrete gesture whose result appears near the pencil tip and is never destructive.
Use barrel roll only to change the mark being made, never for navigation or showing controls.
Allow writing anywhere text entry feels natural, including custom fields, without a tap to focus first.
While people write, keep the field still, do not autoscroll, and hide placeholder and autocompletion text.
Give handwriting enough room by enlarging a field before writing starts or during a pause, never mid-stroke.
Keep markup colors fixed when drawing over a PDF or photo, and add undo and redo buttons in compact layouts where the tool picker lacks them.

ios-inputs|Camera Control.summary: A hardware control on recent iPhone models that opens the camera experience and adjusts camera settings through a system overlay.

rules.rule: Use a slider for a range of values and a picker for discrete options, and add the system zoom and exposure controls where they fit.
Represent each control with an SF Symbol that describes what it does, since custom symbols are not supported.
Keep control names short, show units with slider values, and define the values people pick most as prominent stops.
Keep your own interface out of the overlay area in both orientations, and do not duplicate overlay controls on screen while it is showing.
Enable only the controls that apply to the current camera mode, and put the most used ones in the middle.
Provide a locked camera capture extension so the control can launch the experience from anywhere.

ios-inputs|Digital Crown.summary: The rotating hardware input on Apple Watch and Apple Vision Pro; on Apple Watch it drives navigation and fine adjustments in apps.

rules.rule: On Apple Vision Pro, leave the Digital Crown to the system for volume, immersion, recentering and returning home.
On Apple Watch, build navigation around turning the crown through vertical lists, tabs and pages, with matching touch interactions as a backup.
Where no navigation is needed, use the crown to inspect or adjust data.
Show a visible response to every turn, at a pace that follows the turning speed and still lets people land on a value.
Keep the default haptic detents unless they clash with the interface, and prefer linear detents for lists with very uneven row heights.

ios-inputs|Eyes.summary: In visionOS, looking at an element targets it; the system highlights it and a gesture such as a tap acts on it, without revealing where people look.

rules.rule: Always offer other ways to interact besides looking, in line with the accessibility features people use.
Keep needed content within a comfortable field of view and at least about a meter away, and avoid making eyes jump far or across depths.
Prefer standard components, which respond to gaze consistently.
Give each interactive item at least 16 points of space around it, or 60 points between centers, so gaze can settle on it.
Cut visual noise and motion near what people are looking at, and avoid repeating patterns that fill the view.
Draw the eye with gentle cues such as placement, contrast or slight motion, and give interactive items rounded shapes.
Give a component made of several parts one containing shape the system can highlight as a whole.
Save custom hover effects for special moments, pick a delay that matches their purpose, keep at least one main view steady, and test them on the device.

ios-inputs|Focus and selection.summary: Focus shows which item keyboard, remote or controller input will act on; selecting acts on it, sometimes in the same step.

rules.rule: Use the system focus effects and create a custom one only when truly necessary.
Never move focus on your own; when the focused item disappears during directional navigation move focus to a neighbor, otherwise hide the indicator.
Follow each platform's reach: on iPadOS and macOS make content elements focusable and leave controls to full keyboard access; on tvOS make every element reachable.
Use a focus ring on text and search fields and a full-row highlight in lists and collections.
On iPadOS, group custom views into focus groups so Tab moves between groups in reading order and arrow keys move within a group.
On iPadOS, shape and position the halo to match the item's contours and keep it unclipped, and raise the priority of the item a group should focus first.
On tvOS, let gestures act on full-screen content instead of moving focus, and avoid a free pointer outside gameplay.
On tvOS, design every focus state (unfocused, focused, pressed, selected, unavailable) and supply assets sharp at the enlarged focused size without crowding neighbors.
On visionOS, support the same focus system for connected keyboards and controllers, keeping it separate from the gaze hover effect.

properties.web: roving tabindex in a composite widget

ios-inputs|Game controls.summary: Input for games: virtual touch controls, physical controllers and keyboard bindings, always with the platform's default input as a fallback.

rules.rule: Prefer touching game objects directly, and add virtual controls only for many actions or movement.
Make main virtual controls at least 44 by 44 points and secondary ones at least 28 by 28, placed within safe areas and clear of system features.
Show a press state that is visible around a finger, backed by sound and haptics.
Use artwork that shows what a button does rather than letters like A or R1, and hide controls that do not apply right now.
Put movement on the left and camera on the right, with a thumbstick that appears where the thumb lands and direct panning for the camera.
Keep the platform's default input working as a fallback, and if a controller is required, detect it and prompt calmly to connect one.
Match on-screen labels and symbols to the controller in use, per player, and prefer symbols to text.
Outside gameplay, follow the platform button conventions: A activates, B goes back, the shoulders switch sections and Menu pauses.
Favor single-key bindings, group related actions on nearby keys, check comfort on an Apple keyboard, and let players remap keys.
On visionOS, make spatial controllers behave like hands: look and press a trigger to act indirectly, reach and press to act directly.

ios-inputs|Gestures.summary: Physical motions such as tap, swipe, drag and pinch that act directly on content, on a touchscreen, a touch surface or in the air.

rules.rule: Never make a gesture the only way to do something; voice, keyboard and Switch Control must reach the same result.
Keep standard gestures meaning what people expect, and do not invent a new gesture for a standard action such as activating or scrolling.
Respond while the gesture is under way, showing how far it has to go and what will happen.
Make it clear when a gesture is unavailable, for example with a distinct locked or disabled state.
Add a custom gesture only for frequent, specialized tasks, and make it discoverable, easy, distinct and never the sole route to an important action.
Treat shortcut gestures as extras next to visible controls, such as an edge swipe beside a Back button, and never take over gestures reserved for system UI.
On iOS and iPadOS, honor the system multi-finger gestures for undo, redo, copy and paste, and allow simultaneous gestures only where play needs them.
On visionOS, support standard indirect gestures everywhere, keep direct touch for close-up objects, and avoid requiring a particular hand, posture or both hands.
On visionOS, keep the area around the hand free for system overlays and avoid custom hand-roll motions that collide with them.
On watchOS, give double tap to the most used button only on screens that do not scroll: never on lists, scrolling content or vertically paged tabs.
Map the standard gestures to their usual results: tap activates, swipe reveals or dismisses, drag moves, hold reveals more, pinch zooms and rotate turns.

properties.web: click on a button or Pressable
pointer events with a Drag handle

ios-inputs|Gyroscope and accelerometer.summary: Motion sensors that report how a device moves and tilts, for activity tracking, games and similar real-world uses.

rules.rule: Read motion data only when it gives people a clear benefit, never just to collect it.
Explain in the permission text why the app needs motion data.
Outside active gameplay, do not drive the interface by tilting or shaking the device.

ios-inputs|Keyboards.summary: Physical keyboards for typing, navigating and running commands through keyboard shortcuts and, in games, key bindings.

rules.rule: Support Full Keyboard Access so every window, menu and control works from the keyboard, and test with it turned on.
On iPadOS, provide keyboard navigation for text, lists and sidebars, and leave controls such as buttons and switches to Full Keyboard Access.
Keep standard shortcuts working as people expect, and give a frequent unique action its own new shortcut.
Do not repurpose a standard shortcut unless its usual command cannot apply in the app at all.
Add custom shortcuts only for the most frequent app-specific commands.
Use Command as the main modifier, Shift as a related secondary, Option rarely and Control not at all, and pair other modifiers only with letters.
List modifiers in the order Control, Option, Shift, Command, and show the upper character of a key rather than adding Shift.
Leave localizing and mirroring of shortcuts to the system, keep the standard modifier meanings during drag and resize, and never extend an existing shortcut with a modifier for something unrelated.
On visionOS, write shortcut titles that make sense in a flat list without submenu context, and allow for the typing overlay a connected keyboard brings up.

ios-inputs|Nearby interactions.summary: Experiences that use the distance and direction of nearby Ultra Wideband devices, such as moving audio by bringing two devices together.

rules.rule: Start from how the task happens in the physical world, and use distance, direction and context to shape the interaction.
Make feedback sharpen as people get closer, keep it continuous, and combine visual, audio and haptic feedback to suit where attention is.
Always offer another way to complete the task.
Guide people, without spelling it out, to hold the device upright, and design for the sensor's limited field of view.
Explain in onboarding that people or objects between devices can weaken the result.
On iPhone, use both distance and direction to guide people toward the other device.
On Apple Watch, rely on distance only, and keep the app in the foreground for the whole interaction.

ios-inputs|Pointing devices.summary: A trackpad or mouse used to point, click and gesture: the main input on a Mac and an extra input on iPad and Apple Vision Pro.

rules.rule: Keep trackpad and mouse gestures behaving as they do across the system, and never redefine systemwide gestures.
Give the same results whether people use touch, eyes, a pointer or a keyboard, including when they hold a modifier key while dragging.
Let the pointer bring back controls that hide or fade, such as a minimized toolbar or video controls.
On iPadOS, support drag-to-select multiple items in custom views, and treat pointer and finger differently only when it adds precision, such as clicking an exact seek point.
On iPadOS, use the system effects as intended: highlight for small transparent elements, lift for small opaque ones, hover for large ones, and the standard pointers for buttons and text.
On iPadOS, pad hit regions by about 12 points around bezeled elements and 24 points around unbezeled ones, keep adjacent bar buttons contiguous, and give a corner radius for nonstandard lift shapes.
On iPadOS, keep custom pointer shapes and accessories simple and useful, use annotations for real values such as dimensions, and never put instructions on the pointer.
On iPadOS, scale on hover only where an element has room to grow, use tint alone in tight spaces, and never add shadow without scale.
On macOS, support the standard clicks and gestures people may customize, with secondary click for context menus, and use the standard pointer shapes for their meanings.
On visionOS, rely on the system to follow gaze for pointer context and to hide the pointer during gestures.

ios-inputs|Remotes.summary: The Siri Remote and compatible remotes, whose clickpad, touch surface and buttons drive navigation and playback on Apple TV.

rules.rule: Use standard gestures for standard actions outside gameplay, and keep focus moving in the direction of the swipe.
Show what a gesture will do, for example a hint when a thumb rests on the surface, and add custom gestures only where they fit, such as in a game.
Use a press for deliberate actions, treat taps as light navigation, and ignore taps during live video since they are easily accidental.
Respond to tap position (up, down, left, right) only where it is intuitive and discoverable.
Make Back open the parent screen, or in a game open and close a pause menu, and make Play/Pause control media playback.
Let swipes scroll with momentum and presses select, with a press before a swipe starting scrubbing.
Map each remote button to its expected app and game behavior, with the touch surface navigating and pressing activating.
In a live-viewing app with a program guide, open it with the guide button and page through it with page up and down, which change channel during playback.

properties.ios: onTapGesture(count:perform:) on a focused view / UIPress type .select

ios-technologies|AirPlay.summary: Wireless streaming of an app's audio and video to Apple TV, HomePod and compatible TVs and speakers.

rules.rule: Play media in the system player, which already includes AirPlay; build a custom player only when the system one cannot do the job.
Offer every available resolution in the stream so a large external screen gets a sharp picture.
Keep playback going when the app moves to the background or the device locks, and never start mirroring on the person's behalf.
Send only the content people chose to watch; keep decorative loops, autoplay previews and other in-app video on the local device.
Keep the rest of the app usable while streaming, and respond to remote play, pause and skip commands.
In a custom player, use Apple's AirPlay symbol in a button that looks and behaves like the system one, with clear states for starting, playing and unavailable.
Show the AirPlay icon and name only as a noninteractive mark, in the same color and treatment as any other technology marks beside it, and less prominent than the app's own brand.
Write AirPlay as one word with capital A and P, and use it as a noun (works with AirPlay), never as a verb.

ios-technologies|Always On.summary: A dimmed, low-power state in which the device keeps showing glanceable app content after people stop interacting with it.

rules.rule: Hide personal and sensitive values, such as balances or health data, whenever the display is in Always On.
Keep the one or two facts people want at a glance readable and dim everything secondary, including large images and color fills.
Keep the layout stable when Always On starts and ends: show controls as unavailable rather than removing them, and update content rarely and quietly.
Let running motion settle smoothly to rest instead of freezing it mid-animation.

ios-technologies|App Clips.summary: A small, instantly available slice of an app or game that finishes one task or offers a demo without a full install.

rules.rule: Let people finish the task or the whole demo inside the App Clip; never require the full app to complete it.
Build a short, linear flow from native components: no tab bar, no settings, as few screens and fields as possible, and no web views.
Open straight onto the part that fits the context, with no splash screen and no waiting for downloads.
Avoid asking for an account up front; if one is needed, ask after the task and keep it short, for example with Sign in with Apple, and offer Apple Pay for payment.
Never use an App Clip only for marketing, and never show ads in it.
Store as little data as possible, keep anything you must keep securely off the device, and never assume earlier data is still there.
Suggest the full app once, politely, when the task is done or at a natural pause, never in the middle of it or through notifications.
Send only notifications that help finish the task the person started; never promotional ones.

rules.section: Creating content for an App Clip card
rules.rule: Give the card a photo or graphic that shows the value, without text or UI screenshots, plus a short title and subtitle and the action verb that fits (View, Play or Open).
Show the generated App Clip Code unaltered, upright, unobstructed, large enough for the scanning distance and on a flat surface with clear space around it.
Test every printed code from several angles before distributing it, and print on matte, high-resolution media.

ios-technologies|Apple In-App Purchase.summary: The system way to sell digital goods inside an app: consumables, permanent unlocks and subscriptions.

rules.rule: Let people use and value the app before asking them to buy, and style the store like the rest of the app.
Show the full billing price of every item, with short product names that fit on one line.
Use the system confirmation sheet unchanged, and hide or explain the store when the person cannot make payments.
Keep the refund action plainly titled and visible without scrolling; help and alternatives may come first but never block the request, and never speak for Apple's refund policy.
Prompt to subscribe at meaningful moments, and never invite someone who is already a subscriber to subscribe again.
On the sign-up screen, state each option's name, duration, what it includes and its localized price, explain what is billed when a trial ends, and offer sign-in or restore for existing subscribers.
Ask only for what signup needs, and also offer a way to subscribe from settings.
Offer a Redeem Code action that opens the system flow, and put newly unlocked content to use as soon as redemption completes.
Make cancelling easy to find, and show the subscription and its next renewal date near the manage action.
On watchOS, show the same required subscription details, in a modal sheet with a close action, laid out so options compare at a glance.

ios-technologies|Apple Pay.summary: Fast, private payment for physical goods, services, donations and recurring charges, in apps and on the web.

rules.rule: Offer Apple Pay wherever it is supported, make it the primary option when the person has a card ready, and hide it where the device cannot use it.
Use an Apple Pay button only to start payment or setup; never hide it or show it disabled, and explain any missing choice after it is tapped.
Keep checkout in one branded flow, lead with Apple Pay, and offer it on product pages and as express checkout.
Collect options, split shipping, pickup location and optional notes before the payment sheet, and ask for an account only after purchase, prefilled from checkout.
Report the transaction result in the payment sheet, then show an order confirmation with next steps.
Request only essential information, use short line items for extra charges, discounts and pending amounts, and name the business that will appear on the statement after Pay.
Let the payment sheet show progress; add no spinners of your own.
Accept reasonable input formats, and name the field and the exact fix in a short error message.
Cancel any payment in progress when the sheet is dismissed by a cancel or timeout.
Before authorizing a recurring payment, make the frequency, trial terms, upfront fees and today's amount clear in line items and the total.
Create Apple Pay buttons with the system API in a type and style that suit the background; never draw or imitate them.
Size the Apple Pay button at least as large as any other payment button, keep it on screen without scrolling, and place it beside or above the add-to-cart action.
Use the Apple Pay mark only to show acceptance among payment options, unaltered apart from height, and never as a button.
Write Apple Pay as two capitalized words in your own typeface, never translated, plural or possessive.

ios-technologies|Augmented reality.summary: Camera-based experiences that place convincing virtual objects in the real world, built on ARKit.

rules.rule: Give the camera view the whole screen, keep text and controls minimal, and put any persistent controls in fixed screen space within easy reach.
Keep people comfortable and safe: avoid long arm-held poses, introduce movement gradually and never encourage sudden or sweeping motion.
State up front what space the experience needs, since people may have little room or no large flat surface.
Use the system coaching view while the scene initializes or relocalizes, and hide unrelated UI meanwhile.
Show when a surface is ready, place the object the moment people ask and refine its position quietly afterward, and point toward objects that are offscreen.
Let people move and rotate objects directly with familiar gestures, accept touches near small targets, and keep objects visible and on their surface while they move.
Never use scaling to fake distance, and offer scaling only when real-world size does not matter.
Use plain words instead of technical AR terms, prefer 3D hints in the scene, and put critical text in screen space.
After an interruption, hide placed objects while relocalizing and offer a way to cancel or restart if it does not succeed.
When tracking struggles, suggest a friendly fix such as more light or slower movement, and always allow a reset.
Use the AR glyph and badges only for ARKit experiences, unaltered, with clear space around them, and badge items only when some items cannot be viewed in AR.

ios-technologies|CareKit.summary: A framework of prebuilt task, chart and contact views and an on-device store for apps that manage care plans.

rules.rule: Publish a clear privacy policy and get permission before reading any data from the device or system.
Ask for health data at the moment it is needed, explain why in the system permission screen, and leave sharing controls to the system settings.
Use each view type, task, chart or contact, only for the content it was designed for.
Pick the task style that fits the action, from one step to a checklist or grid, and describe it accurately in as few words as possible.
Color may reinforce the kind of task, but never carry meaning on its own.
Keep chart labels short, use clearly distinct, high-contrast colors with a legend when needed, state the time unit, and group large data sets.
Send few notifications, combine items where possible, and let people complete tasks from the notification detail.
Prefer the built-in symbols, design any custom symbol around health rather than decoration or a logo, and keep branding subtle and free of advertising.

ios-technologies|CarPlay.summary: Shows an iPhone app on a car's built-in display through system templates designed for use while driving.

rules.rule: Never require the iPhone while CarPlay is active: the app works with the phone locked and out of reach, and any setup happens before driving.
Start playback only when people choose to, open the audio session only when sound is ready, and resume after an interruption only if it was temporary.
Balance your own audio levels if needed, but leave the overall volume to the person.
Show Now Playing as soon as audio can play, loading descriptive details afterward.
Show only high-value content that can be scanned from the driver's seat, with the most important, largest targets in the upper half.
Use a small palette, keep interactive and static elements different in color, and test in a real car in daylight, at night, and in light and dark appearances.
Supply @2x and @3x artwork and reuse the iPhone app icon, lightening any black background.
Report only errors that matter, on the car display, never asking people to pick up the phone.

ios-technologies|Game Center.summary: Apple's social gaming service for achievements, leaderboards, challenges and multiplayer, shown through GameKit's system UI or your own.

rules.rule: Check for a signed-in player at launch and set up Game Center right then.
Show the access point on menu and settings screens only, never during play, splash screens or tutorials, keep controls clear of both its sizes, and pause the game while the overlay is open.
In custom links, use Apple's Game Center artwork unaltered and Game Center's own terms for its features.
Map achievements to the system states, upload them in a meaningful order, and keep titles and descriptions within two lines each.
Give every achievement its own rich image with the subject centered for the circular mask.
Choose classic or recurring boards to suit the goal, group many boards into sets, and give each a distinct image that survives cropping.
Make challenges short, skill-based and scored on the latest attempt, and deep-link straight to the right level, after any needed tutorial.
Support party codes: let players see and type the code, and join late, leave early and come back.
On watchOS, expect Game Center content to appear on the paired iPhone; there is no system Game Center UI on the watch.

ios-technologies|Generative AI.summary: Features that use models to create or transform text, images and other content, designed responsibly and with people in control.

rules.rule: Keep people in charge: let them dismiss, undo or retry any generated change, and mark clearly where AI is used.
Ask for personal attributes rather than inferring them, and test with diverse people to catch stereotypes.
Add generative features only where they clearly help, and keep a non-AI path when the feature is unavailable or declined.
Never present AI output or an AI agent as human, and state what the feature can and cannot do, with suggested prompts to start.
Get permission before using personal data, use the minimum, offer an opt-out, and say plainly what leaves the device, what is stored and whether it trains a model.
Warn that output may contain errors, avoid asking the model for facts it cannot verify, and confirm before any destructive or hard-to-undo action.
Put Edit, Undo, Retry or Adjust next to the result and confirm when a correction takes effect.
During generation, describe what is actually happening rather than a generic busy message, and offer several distinct results when a choice helps.
When a request is blocked or the result is poor, explain why and suggest a better request.
Offer a quick, optional, nonintrusive way to rate output, such as thumbs up and down, with room for detail.

ios-technologies|HealthKit.summary: The shared store for health and fitness data that an app may read from and write to with the person's permission.

rules.rule: Request health data only if the app has a real health purpose, at the moment the data is needed, and every time access is needed.
Explain the reason and benefit in the system permission screen, never in a copy of it, and leave all sharing controls to the system settings.
Use Activity rings only for one identified person's Move, Exercise and Stand progress, never as decoration, branding or another ring-shaped chart.
Show the rings with their own colors and background, unfiltered and uncropped, with an outer margin at least the gap between rings.
Keep notifications about activity specific to your app; never repeat the system's progress updates or show the rings in them.
Use Apple's Health icon unaltered, with the name Apple Health beside it, only to show compatibility, never as a button or in place of a word.
Call it Apple Health or the Apple Health app in people-facing text; HealthKit is a developer term.

ios-technologies|HomeKit.summary: Secure control of home accessories through the Home app, Siri and accessory apps that share one model of homes, rooms and zones.

rules.rule: Use HomeKit's object model and terms, scene rather than action set and descriptive names rather than service or characteristic, and show an accessory's home, room and zone in its detail view.
Defer to the setup people made in the Home app; never ask them to set up their home again or show duplicate home settings.
Start with the system setup flow, add any custom tour afterward, explain why Home data is needed, and make accounts and other platforms optional.
Suggest service names that work well with Siri, check renamed services against HomeKit's naming rules, and steer room names out of service names.
After setup, show example Siri phrases using the chosen names, and offer shortcuts only for features HomeKit itself cannot do.
Reflect changes made elsewhere automatically, and never write to the Home database without the person's clear intent.
Leave camera images unobstructed, and offer a talk button only for cameras that support two-way audio.
Use Apple's HomeKit icon unaltered and noninteractive, matched to the color and treatment of other technology marks.

rules.section: Referencing HomeKit and the Home app
rules.rule: Write HomeKit and Apple Home with their exact capitalization, untranslated, less prominent than your brand, and as compatibility (works with HomeKit), never as the actor.

ios-technologies|iCloud.summary: Keeps people's documents, data and app state current on all their devices without any manual syncing.

rules.rule: Work with iCloud automatically; if a choice is needed, ask once at first launch whether to use it for everything or nothing, never per document.
Keep content current, but for very large files let people choose when to download, show that a newer version exists, and give quiet progress for slow updates.
Store only what people created and understand; never fill their paid storage with app resources or data you can regenerate.
When iCloud is off or unreachable, skip the alert and note quietly that changes will not reach other devices yet.
Warn before deleting a document that the deletion reaches every device, and ask for confirmation.
Resolve version conflicts automatically where possible, otherwise early and with a clear, unobtrusive choice; sync useful app state and include iCloud content in search.

ios-technologies|ID Verifier.summary: Lets an iPhone app read a mobile ID in person, sharing only the data the check needs.

rules.rule: Request only what the check needs, such as an over-age threshold rather than a birth date.
Register your organization so its official name and logo appear on the customer's device during the request.
Start verification with a plainly labeled button such as Verify Age or Verify Identity, without NFC or QR symbols and never with the Apple logo.
For a display-only check, give the verifier clear match and no-match buttons to record the result.

ios-technologies|iMessage apps and stick.summary: Apps and sticker packs that live inside Messages conversations for sharing, collaborating and decorating.

rules.rule: Offer one primary, instantly clear experience per iMessage app, often content from the main app that is worth sharing or deciding on together.
Put the most-used items in the compact view and keep text editing to the expanded view.
Design stickers that stay legible on any background and when scaled or rotated, and that suit a wide range of people.
Give every sticker a localized accessibility description.
Use one sticker size for the whole pack and keep each file within the size limit.
Supply square-cornered icons in every required size and let the system round them.

ios-technologies|Live Photos.summary: Photos that carry a few seconds of motion and sound around the moment of capture.

rules.rule: Apply edits to every frame, or offer to convert the Live Photo to a still.
Keep a Live Photo whole; never split out its frames or audio.
When sharing, let people preview the full Live Photo and always offer to send it as a still.
Show download progress and when the photo becomes playable, and show a still where Live Photos are unsupported.
Signal a Live Photo with a hint of motion or the system badge in a consistent corner, never with a play button.
In visionOS, expect people to view Live Photos but not capture them.

ios-technologies|Mac Catalyst.summary: Builds a Mac app from an iPad app, which then has to adopt Mac conventions rather than just run in a window.

rules.rule: Prepare the iPad app first with drag and drop, keyboard navigation and shortcuts, resizable multitasking layouts and multiple windows, and reconsider if it depends on hardware the Mac lacks.
Start with the scaled iPad idiom and move to the Mac idiom once the app feels at home, auditing layout, text sizes and images, ideally with a separate asset catalog.
Use text styles and flexible sizes instead of fixed font, view or layout sizes, and limit appearance changes to those macOS controls support.
Replace an iPad tab bar with a sidebar split view, or a segmented control for flat content, list top-level items in the View menu, and add Next and Previous buttons alongside swipes.
Make a macOS version of the app icon.
Use the wider window: split single columns, show inspectors beside content instead of in popovers, and move key controls from the bottom and side edges into the toolbar.
Put every command in the menu bar with its keyboard shortcut, and give each object a context menu of relevant actions.

ios-technologies|Machine learning.summary: Features that learn from data and use, such as recommendations or recognition, designed to set expectations and recover from mistakes.

rules.section: The role of machine learning in your app
rules.rule: Decide whether the feature is critical or complementary, uses private data, acts proactively, is visible and improves dynamically, and hold critical, sensitive and proactive features to the highest accuracy.
Ask for feedback rarely and always optionally, label each option by its effect (show fewer of these) rather than a vague dislike, and apply and remember it at once.
Protect behavioral data, tell people how it is gathered and shared, let them limit it, and do not base suggestions on private or sensitive topics.
Combine several recent signals, keep room for discovery, and update suggestions at a pace that matches how people use the feature.
Calibrate only when the feature cannot work without it: once, quickly, with a clear goal and progress, help when stuck, a success state, cancel at any time and a way to edit the data later.
Match the remedy to how serious a mistake is, make predictable mistakes easy to fix, and take extra care with proactive features.
Use familiar controls for corrections, show the corrected result immediately and remember it, prefer guided alternatives, and never rely on corrections to excuse poor results.
Offer a few clearly different options on one screen, most likely first, with a short note on what sets each apart.
Show confidence only once it is known to track quality, express it as plain categories, ordering or advice rather than raw numbers, and hold back low-confidence suggestions.
Explain a result by its factual basis, neither too vague nor too specific, without jargon or claims about people's feelings.
Set expectations early, show how to get good results, explain poor ones, suggest alternatives instead of empty results, and announce when a limitation is gone.

ios-technologies|Maps.summary: An interactive map of outdoor or indoor places with annotations, overlays, routes and place cards.

rules.rule: Keep the map interactive, with the familiar zoom, pan and rotate, and do not cover it with static elements.
Use the default emphasis for a standard map and the muted one when rich custom content must stand out.
Offer search with category filters, mark the selected element with a distinct outline and color, and cluster nearby points that would overlap.
The map's Apple attribution and legal notice stay on screen, attached to the map, inset from its edges and above any sliding panel at rest.
Tint annotations to the app's colors with an icon or at most two or three characters, and use overlays at the level that shows or hides what lies beneath as intended.
Give custom controls enough contrast against the map, with a thin stroke or light shadow if needed.

rules.section: Displaying place cards in a map
rules.rule: Choose a place card style that fits the map's size and does not repeat information shown elsewhere, and keep the selected place visible beside it.

rules.section: Adding place cards outside of a map
rules.rule: Include a map in any place card shown outside a map, and cue that a place can be opened, for example with a pin icon or a details button.
Reveal detail as people zoom in, style areas with color plus icons, add a concise floor picker for several levels, dim surrounding context, and keep the venue on screen.
On watchOS, fit the static map on screen without scrolling and show the smallest region that holds every point of interest.

properties.ios: Marker or Annotation in Map / MKMarkerAnnotationView
MapPolygon, MapPolyline, MapCircle / MKOverlay with MKOverlayLevel

ios-technologies|NFC.summary: Reads data from electronic tags on nearby real-world objects, in the app or in the background.

rules.rule: Ask people to hold the device near or scan an object, not to tap or touch it.
Avoid technical terms such as NFC or tag in people-facing text.
Write scanning-sheet instructions as one short, complete sentence that names the object, updated for each following scan.
Always offer in-app scanning as well, for devices without background reading.

ios-technologies|Photo editing.summary: Extensions that edit photos and videos inside the Photos app, saving results without losing the original.

rules.rule: When people cancel after making edits, confirm first and say the edits will be lost; skip this when nothing has changed.
Use the toolbar the system provides; never add a second top toolbar.
Let people preview the result before returning to Photos, and use your app icon as the extension icon.

ios-technologies|ResearchKit.summary: A framework of ready-made screens for medical research apps: onboarding, consent, surveys, active tasks and participant profiles.

rules.rule: Run onboarding in a fixed order: introduction, eligibility, informed consent, then data permissions.
State the study's subject and purpose with a clear call to action, and let existing participants sign in and continue.
Check eligibility early, ask only for required criteria in plain language, and make answers easy to enter.
Split consent into short plain-language sections with more detail on request, make the whole form viewable before agreement, and then collect the signature.
Request only data essential to the study, explaining why each kind is needed.
Keep surveys short with one question per screen, state their length up front, show progress and confirm completion; describe active tasks simply with their requirements and a clear end.

rules.section: Managing personal information and providing encouragement
rules.rule: Keep a profile for editing data, viewing consent and leaving the study, and a dashboard that shows progress, both reachable at all times.

ios-technologies|SharePlay.summary: Lets people do an app activity together in real time from their own devices, kept in sync alongside FaceTime or Messages.

rules.rule: Use SharePlay for live, same-moment activities, and offer a way to save or share the result for anyone who continues later.
Choose between one shared view for watching or browsing and per-person views where roles differ, and make it work across Apple platforms.
Start activities from a recognizable button with the SharePlay symbol, and bring joiners straight to the shared content, handling sign-in or purchase in a view that closes when done.
Describe each activity briefly in the invitation, and show who changed what when one person's action affects everyone.
Use SharePlay as a noun or a button verb, never with an adjective or an inflected form.
On iPhone, iPad and Mac, let shared video keep playing in Picture in Picture or its own window.

In visionOS, prefer starting from a window, keep everyone's views in sync unless a personal view adds value, let people opt in to immersion changes mid-task, keep comfort settings per person, and make leaving and rejoining easy.
In visionOS, pick a spatial template per stage of the activity, change seats only after someone acts, keep roles independent of seats, and support people who have no spatial Persona.

ios-technologies|ShazamKit.summary: Recognizes audio by matching a sample against the Shazam catalog or your own.

rules.rule: Explain why the microphone is needed, and stop recording as soon as the sample is captured.
Ask before saving recognized songs to the person's iCloud library.

ios-technologies|Sign in with Apple.summary: Private, fast sign-in and sign-up with an Apple Account, in apps and on the web, without new passwords or forms.

rules.rule: Ask people to sign in only when it brings clear value, as late as possible, and in commerce only after the purchase.
Offer to link an existing account, welcome people straight into the new account, and show the sign-in method in account settings.
Never ask for a password, and never ask for a personal email address when someone chose a private relay address.
Keep extra data requests to a minimum, mark each as required or optional, explain why, and never block features when optional data is declined.
Show people the data they shared, for example by greeting them with it.
Size the Sign in with Apple button at least as large as any other sign-in option, and keep it on screen without scrolling.
Prefer the system button, with one title variant used consistently and the white, outlined or black style that contrasts with the background.

rules.section: Creating a custom Sign in with Apple button
rules.rule: A custom button stays instantly recognizable: Apple's logo artwork uncropped at button height, an approved title, black or white only, keeping the standard proportions and margins.

ios-technologies|Siri.summary: The system assistant, which can run an app's actions and reach its content once the app exposes them through App Intents.

rules.section: Getting your app to work with Siri
rules.rule: Expose the app's key actions and content as intents and entities, and adopt a matching schema domain where one exists.
Tell the system what is on screen, index personally relevant content, and donate actions people take so Siri can suggest them later.
Start from the most-used actions and their contexts, name them in words people already use, and share relevant content rather than everything.
Never put ads, marketing or purchase pitches in anything Siri delivers, and add custom responses only where the built-in ones fall short.

rules.section: Customizing your app’s experience with Siri
rules.rule: Write responses that are short, specific and work both spoken and on screen, without the app name, device-specific wording, needless pronouns or jokes.

rules.section: Customizing your app’s experience with Siri
rules.rule: Ask an open question when the list of choices is too long to read, and make errors specific to what went wrong.
Call Siri by name, never by a pronoun; never imitate Siri or use its reserved phrases, and never translate the name.

ios-technologies|Tap to Pay on iPhone.summary: Lets a merchant accept contactless cards and wallets on an iPhone, with no extra hardware.

rules.section: Enabling Tap to Pay on iPhone
rules.rule: Have an administrator accept the terms before any customer flow, and tell other users that admin access is needed.
Offer a short tutorial on each payment type, card positioning and PIN entry, easy to find again later.
Always show the Tap to Pay on iPhone option in checkout, even while it configures, with progress, and prepare it at launch and each return to the foreground.
Name the action Tap to Pay on iPhone, shortened to Tap to Pay where space is short; style it like the app's other buttons and leave out the Apple logo.
Settle tips and other options that change the total before opening the payment screen, and let merchants switch to their other readers within checkout.
Show progress while authorizing, then a clear approved or declined result with a receipt option, and another way to pay when a tap fails.
Use a generic label such as Look Up or Refund for card reads with no amount, and keep loyalty-card flows separate and free of payment wording.

ios-technologies|VoiceOver.summary: The built-in screen reader, which speaks the interface to people who cannot see the screen.

rules.rule: Give every key element, and every custom one, a descriptive label that stays current as the interface changes.
Describe meaningful images by what they alone convey, and hide purely decorative images.
Summarize what each chart shows and make its interactions available to VoiceOver too.
Give every screen a unique title and accurate section headings.
Group related elements, such as an image and its caption, so they are read together in reading order.
Announce visible content and layout changes.
Expose headings, links and other content types to the rotor.
In visionOS, expect custom gestures to receive no hand input while VoiceOver runs, and keep every action reachable another way.

ios-technologies|Wallet.summary: Holds people's cards, passes, IDs and order tracking, and lets an app add passes, track orders and verify identity.

rules.rule: Offer to add a new pass the moment it is created, add related passes as one group, and suggest an outside-made pass once only.
Show an Add to Apple Wallet button where pass details appear and a View in Wallet link once it is added.
Set expiration, relevance and voided data correctly, keep passes current, ask before deleting one, and send change messages only for time-critical updates.
Design a clean pass rather than a copy of the physical card: key facts in the header, details on the information sheet, brand colors for recognition and legible text.
Never rely on elements another device may drop, and use wording that makes sense on every device.
Choose the pass style that matches its use: boarding pass, coupon, event ticket, store card or a generic style.
Use images for visuals only, never for text or barcodes, keep files small, and supply a pass icon.
Add orders to Wallet right after purchase, provide what is known immediately, keep status current, and use opaque 300 by 300 logo and product images with short localized text.
Describe every item, link to order management and the carrier, give several contact methods, avoid duplicate notifications, and explain any issue or cancellation plainly.
Show Verify with Apple Wallet only where supported, at the moment of need, asking for the minimum data with a clear purpose and stated retention.
On Apple Watch, expect passes to show fewer fields and cropped images, with the rest in a scrolling detail view.
